lis.rossio: Rossio, officially Pedro IV Square, has been Lisbon's main meeting place since the Middle Ages. It hosted bullfights, celebrations and, darkly, the public trials of the Inquisition. After the great earthquake of 1755 the Marquis of Pombal rebuilt the whole Baixa on a strict grid, and Rossio became its northern gate. Look down at the black-and-white wave pattern of the Portuguese pavement, laid in the 1840s and copied from Rio de Janeiro to Macau. The column in the middle carries King Pedro IV, and the D. Maria II National Theatre closes the north side. To the west, the neo-Manueline Rossio railway station, with its two horseshoe doors, hides the platforms for trains to Sintra.
lis.comercio: Praça do Comércio stands on the site of the royal Ribeira Palace, destroyed with its library and archives by the 1755 earthquake and tsunami. Pombal turned the ruins into a vast open square facing the Tagus, framed by yellow arcaded buildings that housed the ministries and the customs. The bronze statue of King José I has stood in the centre since 1775. The triumphal Arch of Rua Augusta, finished only in 1875, shows figures of Portuguese heroes, and you can climb it for a view over the Baixa. On the river side, the Cais das Colunas marble steps were once the ceremonial entrance to the city for kings and ambassadors arriving by boat. In 1908 King Carlos I was assassinated here.
lis.se: Lisbon Cathedral, the Sé, was begun in 1147, right after Afonso Henriques took the city from the Moors, probably on the site of the main mosque. Its two crenellated towers and thick walls make it look more like a fortress than a church, which was deliberate in a frontier city. Inside, the Romanesque nave is plain and solemn, with later Gothic and Baroque additions. Tradition says Saint Anthony of Lisbon, known to the world as Anthony of Padua, was baptised here in 1195. The paid cloister reveals excavations with Roman streets, Moorish houses and medieval walls, a cross-section of two thousand years of the city. The cathedral survived several earthquakes, though the 1755 quake destroyed its Gothic chancel.
lis.santa-luzia: The Santa Luzia viewpoint sits on the old Moorish wall above Alfama, the city's oldest neighbourhood, a maze of alleys that survived the 1755 earthquake largely intact. The small church of Santa Luzia belongs to the Order of Malta, and its outer walls carry two tile panels: one shows the Praça do Comércio before the earthquake, the other the Christian conquest of Lisbon in 1147. Bougainvillea covers the pergola, and from the terrace you see the white dome of the National Pantheon, the bell towers of São Vicente and the river widening into the Straw Sea. A few steps further, the Portas do Sol terrace offers an even wider view. In the evening, fado drifts up from the taverns below.
lis.graca: The Graça viewpoint, officially named after the poet Sophia de Mello Breyner Andresen, stands in front of the Augustinian convent of Graça, founded in the thirteenth century. Graça was one of Lisbon's first suburbs outside the walls, and it still feels like a village: kiosks, old men playing cards and the rattle of tram 28. From under the umbrella pines you look straight across at São Jorge Castle, down over the Baixa grid and out to the 25 de Abril Bridge, the red suspension bridge inspired by San Francisco's. The view faces west, so late afternoon is the best time. A short walk north, the Senhora do Monte viewpoint is the highest in the city and often almost empty.
lis.carmo: The Carmo Convent was Lisbon's largest Gothic church until the morning of 1 November 1755, when the earthquake brought its roof down on the faithful at Mass. It was never rebuilt, and its bare arches against the sky are now the most moving memorial of the disaster; inside is a small archaeological museum. The square outside, with its fountain and jacaranda trees, was where the Carnation Revolution ended on 25 April 1974, when the dictator Marcelo Caetano surrendered at the police barracks. A few steps away, Chiado was the elegant literary quarter: Café A Brasileira, opened in 1905, keeps a bronze statue of the poet Fernando Pessoa at its terrace, and Bertrand, founded in 1732, is considered the oldest operating bookshop in the world.
lis.sao-pedro: The São Pedro de Alcântara viewpoint is a two-level garden on the edge of Bairro Alto, laid out in the nineteenth century over an old rubbish dump. The upper terrace has busts of Greek gods and a tiled map naming every monument you can see across the valley: São Jorge Castle, Graça, the Sé and the Baixa below. You can reach it by the Glória funicular, which has climbed the steep street from Restauradores since 1885. Behind you, Bairro Alto was planned in the sixteenth century as an orderly residential quarter; today its narrow streets are quiet by day and fill with bars and fado houses at night. Just north is the Príncipe Real garden with its giant cedar.
lis.jeronimos: The Jerónimos Monastery was commissioned by King Manuel I around 1501, on the spot where Vasco da Gama and his crew spent their last night before sailing to India in 1497. It was paid for by a tax on the spice trade, and its stone lacework of ropes, sea creatures and armillary spheres made it the masterpiece of the Manueline style. Vasco da Gama and the poet Luís de Camões lie in its church, and the cloister is one of the most beautiful in Europe. The monastery and the nearby tower are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Next door, the Pastéis de Belém bakery has sold custard tarts since 1837, using a recipe that came from the monks and is still kept secret.
lis.torre-belem: The Tower of Belém was built between 1514 and 1520 as a fortress guarding the mouth of the Tagus, and as a ceremonial gateway to Lisbon for ships returning from Africa, India and Brazil. It originally stood on a small island in the river; the 1755 earthquake and later land reclamation moved the shore up to its walls. Look for the Moorish-style watchtowers, the shields of the Order of Christ and, on the western side, a stone rhinoceros, thought to be the first sculpture of one in Europe, inspired by a rhino sent to King Manuel in 1515. On the way you pass the Padrão dos Descobrimentos, a 1960 monument shaped like a caravel prow, with Henry the Navigator leading the explorers.

opo.aliados: The Avenida dos Aliados is Porto's grand civic avenue, named after the Allies of the First World War. It was laid out in the 1910s and 1920s by demolishing an old neighbourhood, and its granite buildings topped with domes and statues, mostly banks and insurance companies, give it a Parisian air. At the top stands the City Hall, finished in 1957, with a 70-metre clock tower. In the middle of the avenue, the equestrian statue of King Pedro IV faces the City Hall. This is where Porto gathers to celebrate football titles and New Year. At the foot of the avenue, the Liberdade Square leads down towards São Bento station, and the Café Imperial, now a fast-food restaurant, keeps its stunning Art Deco stained glass.
opo.clerigos: The Clérigos Tower was designed by the Italian architect Nicolau Nasoni and completed in 1763. At 75 metres it was for a long time the tallest building in Portugal and served as a landmark for ships entering the Douro; 225 steps lead to the top, with a view over the whole city. The Baroque church below has an unusual oval nave. A short walk away, the Livraria Lello opened its neo-Gothic building in 1906; its red forked staircase, carved wooden ceilings and stained-glass skylight made it one of the most famous bookshops in the world. Legend links it to J. K. Rowling, who lived in Porto in the early 1990s, though she has said she never visited it.
opo.sao-bento: São Bento railway station was built on the site of a sixteenth-century Benedictine convent and opened in 1916. Its atrium is lined with about 20,000 blue-and-white azulejo tiles painted by Jorge Colaço between 1905 and 1916. The panels tell the history of Portugal: the arrival of King João I and Philippa of Lancaster in Porto, the conquest of Ceuta in 1415, and the battle of Arcos de Valdevez, while the upper frieze shows the history of transport and scenes of rural life in the north. Look for the wedding procession and the pilgrimage to a country fair. Trains still leave from here for the Douro valley, one of the most beautiful rail journeys in Europe.
opo.se-porto: Porto Cathedral stands on the Pena Ventosa hill, the highest point of the old town, where the city began. Its fortified Romanesque structure dates from the twelfth century, but it was heavily reworked in the Baroque period; Nicolau Nasoni added the loggia on the north side. In 1387 King João I married Philippa of Lancaster here, sealing the alliance with England that is the oldest still in force in the world. The Gothic cloister is lined with eighteenth-century tiles depicting the Song of Songs. The terrace in front, with a twisted stone pillory, gives a view over the rooftops of Ribeira, the Douro and the port wine lodges of Vila Nova de Gaia on the opposite bank.
opo.ponte-luis: The Dom Luís I Bridge was opened in 1886 and designed by Théophile Seyrig, a German-born engineer who had worked with Gustave Eiffel, which is why it is often mistakenly credited to Eiffel himself. At 172 metres, its iron arch was the longest of its kind in the world when built. It has two decks: the lower one for cars and pedestrians at river level, and the upper one, 45 metres above the water, now used by the metro and pedestrians. Walking across the top deck is one of the great experiences of Porto. On the Gaia side, the terrace of the Serra do Pilar monastery, a round church from the sixteenth century, offers the classic postcard view of the city.
opo.ribeira: Ribeira is Porto's medieval riverside quarter, a tangle of narrow alleys and tall, narrow houses painted in faded colours, with laundry hanging from wrought-iron balconies. For centuries it was the heart of the city's trade, where boats unloaded goods and fishermen sold their catch. The arcaded Praça da Ribeira, with its modern cube sculpture, opens onto the quay. Along the river you see the rabelos, flat-bottomed boats that once brought barrels of wine down the Douro from the vineyards to the lodges in Gaia. Ribeira is part of the historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. At sunset the terraces fill up and the Dom Luís I Bridge lights up above the river.
opo.foz: Foz do Douro is where the Douro river meets the Atlantic Ocean, about five kilometres west of the centre. It was once a fishing village and became a fashionable seaside resort for Porto's bourgeoisie in the nineteenth century. You can get there on tram 1, which follows the river from Infante, one of the oldest tram lines in Europe. At the river mouth stand the Felgueiras lighthouse and the São João da Foz fortress, built in the sixteenth century to protect the harbour. The ocean promenade, with its pergola from the early twentieth century, stretches north along rocky beaches and cafés. On rough days, the waves crash spectacularly against the pier, a favourite sight for locals.

mad.sol: Puerta del Sol takes its name from a fifteenth-century gate in the old city wall that faced the rising sun. It is the symbolic centre of Spain: in front of the Royal Post Office building, a plaque in the pavement marks Kilometre Zero, the point from which the country's radial roads are measured. On New Year's Eve, millions of Spaniards watch the clock on that building and eat twelve grapes, one for each stroke of midnight. On 2 May 1808 Madrid rose here against Napoleon's troops, a scene later painted by Goya. Look for the bronze statue of the bear and the strawberry tree, the symbol of Madrid, and the equestrian statue of King Carlos III, known as the best mayor of Madrid.
mad.plaza-mayor: The Plaza Mayor was completed in 1619 under King Felipe III, whose equestrian statue stands in the centre. Surrounded by uniform three-storey buildings with 237 balconies, it was the stage for royal proclamations, bullfights, executions and the autos-da-fé of the Inquisition. It burned three times; after the 1790 fire the architect Juan de Villanueva rebuilt it closed on all four sides, as it is today. The Casa de la Panadería, the old bakers' guild with its painted façade, dominates the north side. Nine arches lead out of the square; the Arco de Cuchilleros descends steep steps to the old knife-makers' street, lined with taverns. At Christmas the square fills with a traditional market of nativity figures.
mad.san-miguel: The Mercado de San Miguel is an iron-and-glass market hall built in 1916, on the site of an older open-air market beside the church of San Miguel. Its cast-iron structure is one of the few surviving examples of this architecture in Madrid. After decades of decline it was restored in 2009 and reinvented as a gourmet food market, where you move from stall to stall tasting tapas: Iberian ham, oysters, croquettes, olives on skewers and vermouth on tap. It can be crowded and pricier than local bars, but it is the easiest place to sample many Spanish specialities in a short time. Nearby, the Cava Baja street is lined with traditional taverns, popular with locals at lunchtime.
mad.palacio-real: The Royal Palace of Madrid was built on the site of the old Moorish fortress and the Alcázar of the Habsburgs, which burned down on Christmas Eve 1734. King Felipe V, the first Bourbon, ordered a new palace in stone so it could not burn again; it was finished in 1764. With over 3,400 rooms it is the largest royal palace in Western Europe by floor area. It is still the official residence of the King of Spain, though used only for state ceremonies. Highlights include the Throne Room with a ceiling by Tiepolo and the Royal Armoury. Opposite stands Almudena Cathedral, begun in 1883 and consecrated only in 1993 by Pope John Paul II, with a colourful modern interior.
mad.debod: The Temple of Debod is a genuine ancient Egyptian temple, more than 2,200 years old, dedicated to the gods Amun and Isis. It originally stood in Nubia, south of Aswan. When the Aswan High Dam threatened to flood it in the 1960s, Spain helped UNESCO save the temples of Abu Simbel, and Egypt gave Debod to Spain as a thank-you gift in 1968. It was dismantled, shipped stone by stone and rebuilt in 1972 in the Parque del Oeste, on the site of the former Montaña barracks, where fierce fighting took place at the start of the Spanish Civil War. The temple keeps its east-west orientation, and at sunset it is reflected in the pool, one of the best views in Madrid.
mad.gran-via: The Gran Vía was opened in stages between 1910 and 1929, cutting through the old city to modernise Madrid; hundreds of buildings were demolished to make way for it. It became the showcase of the new century, with early skyscrapers, cinemas, hotels and department stores in every style from Beaux-Arts to Art Deco. The Telefónica building, completed in 1929, was one of the first skyscrapers in Europe and served as an observation post during the Civil War. At its eastern end, the Metrópolis building, with its slate dome crowned by a winged Victory, is the most photographed corner in Madrid. Today the avenue is known as Madrid's Broadway, for its musical theatres and lively nights.
mad.prado: The Museo del Prado opened in 1819 in a neoclassical building designed by Juan de Villanueva, originally intended as a natural history museum. It holds the collections assembled by the Spanish monarchs over three centuries and is one of the greatest art museums in the world. Its stars are Velázquez, whose Las Meninas is considered one of the most analysed paintings in history; Goya, from his royal portraits to the dark Black Paintings; and El Greco. You will also find Bosch's Garden of Earthly Delights, Rubens, Titian and Dürer. The Paseo del Prado and the Retiro are a UNESCO World Heritage Site called the Landscape of Light, the first urban boulevard of its kind in Europe.
mad.retiro: The Retiro Park was created in the 1630s as a garden for a royal palace of King Felipe IV, the Buen Retiro, of which only two buildings survive. It opened to the public in 1868 and today covers 125 hectares in the heart of Madrid. At the large artificial lake you can rent a rowing boat in front of the monument to King Alfonso XII. The Crystal Palace, an iron-and-glass pavilion built in 1887 for an exhibition on the Philippines, now hosts contemporary art. Look for the Rose Garden, the Fallen Angel fountain, said to be one of the very few public statues of the devil, and the Puerta de Alcalá, the neoclassical gate at the park's north-west corner.

bcn.catalunya: Plaça de Catalunya is the hinge between Barcelona's medieval old town and the nineteenth-century Eixample grid. Until the 1850s this was open land outside the city walls; when the walls came down, the engineer Ildefons Cerdà designed the expansion, and the square took shape in the early twentieth century. Its fountains, statues and mosaic compass rose are surrounded by banks and the El Corte Inglés department store, whose ninth-floor terrace offers a free view. The metro, the regional trains and the airport bus all stop here. From the square, La Rambla leads down to the sea, Passeig de Gràcia leads up towards Gaudí's houses, and Portal de l'Àngel is the city's busiest shopping street.
bcn.rambla: La Rambla follows the bed of an old seasonal stream that ran along the outside of the thirteenth-century city wall. It became a promenade in the eighteenth century and is now a 1.2-kilometre tree-lined avenue running down to the old port. Halfway down, the Boqueria market, whose iron roof dates from 1914, sells fruit, ham, seafood and spices; the best bars are at the back. Further on, step on the Joan Miró mosaic in the pavement, and look at the Liceu opera house, rebuilt after the fire of 1994. At the end, the Columbus Monument points out to sea. The Rambla is lively but crowded; keep your bag in front of you, as pickpockets are common.
bcn.gotic: The Gothic Quarter is the oldest part of Barcelona, built over the Roman colony of Barcino, founded in the first century BC. You can still see sections of the Roman wall and, hidden inside a building on Carrer del Paradís, four columns of the Temple of Augustus. The Cathedral of the Holy Cross and Saint Eulalia was built mostly between the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries; its neo-Gothic façade was only finished in 1913. Its cloister is home to thirteen white geese, one for each year of Saint Eulalia's life. Around it, Plaça Sant Jaume houses the Catalan government and the city hall, the two powers facing each other, and the Plaça del Rei recalls the medieval royal palace.
bcn.santa-maria: Santa Maria del Mar was built in just 54 years, between 1329 and 1383, which gives it a rare unity of style: it is considered the purest example of Catalan Gothic. It was not paid for by kings or bishops but by the people of the seafaring Ribera district; porters carried the stones on their backs from the royal quarry of Montjuïc, a story told in the novel The Cathedral of the Sea. Inside, slender octagonal columns 13 metres apart create an extraordinary sense of space. The church burned for eleven days in 1936, at the start of the Civil War, which is why the interior is so bare. Around it, El Born is full of boutiques, tapas bars and the Picasso Museum.
bcn.sagrada: The Basilica of the Sagrada Família was begun in 1882, and Antoni Gaudí took over the project in 1883, devoting the rest of his life to it. When he died in 1926, hit by a tram, less than a quarter was built. Funded only by donations and tickets, construction continues to this day. In 2025 the central tower of Jesus Christ made it the tallest church in the world, and the tower was due to be completed in 2026, the centenary of Gaudí's death. The Nativity façade, the part Gaudí saw completed, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Inside, columns branch like trees and the stained glass bathes the nave in colour. Pope Benedict XVI consecrated it as a basilica in 2010.
bcn.batllo: Passeig de Gràcia is the grand boulevard of the Eixample, where wealthy families competed to build the most daring modernist houses around 1900. The Casa Batlló, remodelled by Gaudí in 1904 to 1906, has a façade of shimmering broken tiles, balconies shaped like masks and a roof that recalls the scaled back of a dragon slain by Saint George. A few blocks up, the Casa Milà, nicknamed La Pedrera, the stone quarry, was Gaudí's last civil work, built from 1906 to 1912, with an undulating stone façade, wrought-iron balconies and a rooftop of warrior-like chimneys. Both are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Next to Casa Batlló, Casa Amatller and Casa Lleó Morera form the so-called Block of Discord.
bcn.barceloneta: La Barceloneta was built in the 1750s on reclaimed land to rehouse residents of the Ribera district, whose homes were demolished for the Ciutadella fortress. Its grid of narrow streets, with small apartments and laundry hanging from balconies, was a fishermen's and sailors' neighbourhood. The beaches you see today are largely the result of the 1992 Olympic Games, when the city cleared industrial sheds and railway lines to open Barcelona to the sea. The promenade leads to Frank Gehry's giant golden fish sculpture at the Olympic Port and to the sail-shaped W Hotel. Try a seafood paella in one of the traditional restaurants, a local speciality since the days when the neighbourhood lived from fishing.

par.notre-dame: Notre-Dame de Paris was begun in 1163 on the Île de la Cité, the island where Paris was born, and took nearly two centuries to complete. It is a masterpiece of French Gothic, famous for its flying buttresses, rose windows and gargoyles. Napoleon was crowned emperor here in 1804, and Victor Hugo's novel The Hunchback of Notre-Dame saved it from decay in the nineteenth century, prompting Viollet-le-Duc's restoration and the addition of the famous spire. On 15 April 2019 a fire destroyed the roof and the spire. After five years of work by some 2,000 craftspeople, the cathedral reopened in December 2024 with a faithful new spire. In the square in front, a bronze plaque marks Point Zero of France's roads.
par.pont-neuf: Despite its name, the New Bridge is the oldest standing bridge in Paris, completed in 1607 under King Henri IV, whose equestrian statue stands at its centre. It was the first Paris bridge without houses on it and with pavements, so Parisians came to stroll, watch street performers and admire the Seine. Its stone masks, called mascarons, show 384 grotesque faces. Just behind, inside the courtyard of the Palace of Justice, hides the Sainte-Chapelle, built by King Louis IX in the 1240s to house relics of the Passion, including the Crown of Thorns. Its upper chapel is enclosed by fifteen stained-glass windows 15 metres high, with more than 1,100 scenes from the Bible, one of the wonders of Gothic art.
par.louvre: The Louvre began as a fortress built by King Philippe Auguste around 1190 to protect Paris; you can still see its foundations underground. It became a royal palace, was enlarged for six centuries, and was abandoned by Louis XIV for Versailles. During the French Revolution, in 1793, it opened as a public museum. Today it is the most visited museum in the world, home to the Mona Lisa, the Venus de Milo and the Winged Victory of Samothrace, among some 35,000 works on display. The glass pyramid by the architect I. M. Pei caused an outcry when it opened in 1989 and is now a symbol of Paris. The courtyards and the pyramid are free to walk around.
par.tuileries: The Tuileries Garden is named after the tile factories that stood here before Queen Catherine de' Medici built a palace in 1564. The palace burned during the Paris Commune in 1871 and was demolished, but the garden, redesigned in 1664 by André Le Nôtre, the gardener of Versailles, survived. Its symmetrical lawns, gravel paths, round ponds with green metal chairs and statues by Maillol make it the archetypal French formal garden. It forms part of the historical axis, the straight line running from the Louvre through the Concorde and the Champs-Élysées to the Arc de Triomphe and La Défense. At its western end, the Orangerie museum displays Monet's huge Water Lilies paintings.
par.concorde: Place de la Concorde is the largest square in Paris. Laid out in the 1750s in honour of King Louis XV, it was renamed Place de la Révolution in 1792, and the guillotine stood here: Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette and Robespierre were among more than a thousand people executed. In 1795 it was renamed Concorde, harmony, as a gesture of reconciliation. At its centre stands the Luxor Obelisk, more than 3,300 years old, a gift from Egypt that arrived in 1833; its gilded cap was added in 1998. From the square the Champs-Élysées begins, nearly two kilometres of avenue climbing to the Arc de Triomphe, where the Tour de France ends and Bastille Day parades take place.
par.arc: The Arc de Triomphe was commissioned by Napoleon in 1806 after his victory at Austerlitz, but it was only completed in 1836, long after his fall. At 50 metres high it stands at the centre of Place Charles-de-Gaulle, where twelve avenues meet in a star, which is why the square was long called l'Étoile. Its sculptures celebrate the armies of the Revolution and the Empire, and the names of 660 generals and battles are carved on its inner walls. Beneath the arch lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier from the First World War, with an eternal flame rekindled every evening at 6:30 pm. Take the underground passage to reach it; never try to cross the roundabout.
par.eiffel: The Eiffel Tower was built by Gustave Eiffel's company for the 1889 World's Fair, marking the centenary of the French Revolution. Many artists denounced it as a monstrous eyesore, and it was meant to be dismantled after twenty years; it survived because it proved useful as a radio antenna. At about 330 metres it was the tallest structure in the world until 1930. Its 18,000 iron parts are held together by 2.5 million rivets, and it is repainted roughly every seven years. The best view of it is from the Trocadéro terrace, across the Seine, where the Palais de Chaillot was built for the 1937 exhibition. Every evening the tower sparkles for five minutes at the start of each hour.
par.montmartre: Montmartre was a village of vineyards and windmills outside Paris until it was annexed in 1860. Its cheap rents attracted artists: Renoir, Toulouse-Lautrec, Van Gogh, Picasso and Modigliani all lived or worked here, and the Bateau-Lavoir studios saw the birth of Cubism. The white Basilica of the Sacré-Cœur, built between 1875 and 1914 in a Romano-Byzantine style, crowns the hill at the highest point in the city, and its stone, which releases calcite when it rains, stays white. From its steps there is a sweeping view over Paris. Behind it, Place du Tertre is full of painters, and the last vineyard of Paris still produces wine, celebrated each October at the harvest festival.

lon.westminster: The Palace of Westminster is home to the two Houses of Parliament, the Commons and the Lords. A royal palace stood here from the eleventh century, but most of it burned down in 1834; the present Gothic Revival building was designed by Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin. Only Westminster Hall, from 1097, with its magnificent hammerbeam roof, survives from the medieval palace. The clock tower, renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012, houses the great bell known as Big Ben, which has struck the hours since 1859. Across the Thames, the London Eye offers views of the whole city. On Parliament Square, statues of Churchill, Mandela and Gandhi face the palace.
lon.abbey: Westminster Abbey has been the coronation church of English monarchs since William the Conqueror in 1066; Charles III was crowned here in 2023. The present Gothic church was begun by Henry III in 1245. Seventeen monarchs are buried here, including Elizabeth I, along with more than three thousand notable people: Isaac Newton, Charles Darwin and Stephen Hawking lie in the nave, and Poets' Corner honours Chaucer, Dickens and Shakespeare. The Tomb of the Unknown Warrior, near the west door, is the only grave in the abbey that no one walks on. Royal weddings, including that of Prince William and Catherine Middleton in 2011, have taken place here. Visiting the interior is paid.
lon.buckingham: Buckingham Palace was built in 1703 as a townhouse for the Duke of Buckingham and bought by King George III in 1761. Queen Victoria was the first monarch to live here, from 1837, and it remains the London residence and office of the sovereign, with 775 rooms. When the Royal Standard flies over the palace, the King is at home. The famous balcony on the east front is where the royal family appears on great occasions. The Changing of the Guard, with soldiers in red tunics and bearskin hats, takes place on selected mornings. In front stands the Victoria Memorial, and behind you St James's Park, with its lake and pelicans, the oldest royal park in London.
lon.trafalgar: Trafalgar Square commemorates the naval victory of 1805, in which Admiral Horatio Nelson defeated the French and Spanish fleets but was killed by a sniper's bullet. Nelson's Column, 52 metres high, was completed in 1843 and is guarded by four bronze lions by Edwin Landseer. The Fourth Plinth, in the north-west corner, displays changing works of contemporary art. On the north side, the National Gallery holds one of the finest collections of European painting, from Van Eyck and Leonardo da Vinci to Turner, Constable and Van Gogh's Sunflowers, and entry is free. To the east stands St Martin-in-the-Fields, a church famous for its concerts, with a café in its crypt.
lon.covent: Covent Garden takes its name from a medieval convent garden belonging to Westminster Abbey. In the 1630s the architect Inigo Jones designed London's first square here, inspired by Italian piazzas, with St Paul's Church, known as the actors' church. For three centuries it was London's main fruit, vegetable and flower market, the setting of Shaw's Pygmalion and the musical My Fair Lady. When the market moved out in 1974, the elegant iron-and-glass market halls were restored as shops, cafés and craft stalls. Street performers entertain crowds under the portico of the church, a tradition dating back to the seventeenth century. The Royal Opera House stands on the north-east corner of the piazza.
lon.st-pauls: St Paul's Cathedral, with its famous dome, was designed by Sir Christopher Wren after the Great Fire of 1666 destroyed the medieval cathedral; it was completed in 1710. The dome, one of the largest in the world, has a Whispering Gallery where a whisper against the wall can be heard on the other side. During the Blitz of the Second World War, the photograph of the dome rising intact above the smoke became a symbol of resistance. Princess Diana and Prince Charles married here in 1981. The steel Millennium Bridge, opened in 2000, crosses the Thames to Tate Modern, a modern art museum in a former power station, with free entry and a view from its top floor.
lon.tower-bridge: Tower Bridge, often mistaken for London Bridge, opened in 1894. It was designed to let tall ships reach the busy Pool of London while allowing traffic to cross: its two bascules, each weighing over a thousand tonnes, still rise around 800 times a year. The Gothic towers hide a steel frame clad in stone so the bridge would harmonise with the Tower of London next to it. The high-level walkways, with glass floors 42 metres above the river, can be visited. Beside it, the Tower of London, begun by William the Conqueror in 1078, has served as royal palace, prison and execution site, and guards the Crown Jewels. Ravens are kept there, as legend says the kingdom will fall if they leave.

rom.coliseu: The Colosseum, officially the Flavian Amphitheatre, was begun by Emperor Vespasian around 72 AD and inaugurated by his son Titus in 80 AD with 100 days of games. It could hold some 50,000 spectators, who entered through 80 numbered arches and could be covered by a huge awning operated by sailors. Gladiator fights, wild animal hunts and public executions took place here for nearly four centuries. Beneath the arena, the hypogeum was a network of tunnels and lifts that raised animals and scenery into view. After the fall of Rome it was used as a quarry and a fortress, and earthquakes brought down the southern side. It is the largest amphitheatre ever built and one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.
rom.foruns: The Roman Forum, in the valley between the Palatine and Capitoline hills, was the political, religious and commercial heart of ancient Rome for a thousand years. Here stood the Senate House, temples, triumphal arches and the Rostra, the platform where orators addressed the people. Julius Caesar was cremated here in 44 BC, and the remains of his temple still stand. Along Via dei Fori Imperiali, opened in 1932, you can see from above the later Imperial Forums built by Caesar, Augustus, Nerva and Trajan, whose 30-metre column is carved with a spiral frieze of his wars in Dacia. Above, the Palatine Hill is where Rome was legendarily founded by Romulus and where the emperors built their palaces.
rom.vittoriano: The Vittoriano, also called the Altar of the Fatherland, was built between 1885 and 1935 to honour Victor Emmanuel II, the first king of a united Italy. Its dazzling white Botticino marble, so unlike Rome's warm tones, earned it nicknames such as the typewriter and the wedding cake. Its construction destroyed part of the medieval quarter on the Capitoline Hill. At its centre is a 12-metre gilded bronze equestrian statue of the king, and below lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, guarded day and night. A glass lift takes you to the terrace of the Quadrigas, one of the best panoramic views in Rome. Behind it, Michelangelo's Piazza del Campidoglio is worth a short climb.
rom.panteao: The Pantheon, rebuilt by Emperor Hadrian around 125 AD on the site of an earlier temple by Agrippa, whose name still appears on the façade, is the best-preserved building of ancient Rome. Its unreinforced concrete dome, 43.3 metres in diameter, remains the largest of its kind in the world, and the height to the oculus equals the diameter, so a perfect sphere would fit inside. The oculus, an open circle nine metres wide, is the only source of light; when it rains, water drains through small holes in the marble floor. Consecrated as a church in 609, it survived intact. The painter Raphael and the first two kings of Italy are buried here. Since 2023 entry costs five euros.
rom.navona: Piazza Navona follows exactly the shape of the Stadium of Domitian, built in 86 AD for athletic contests, and its houses stand on the ancient stands. In the seventeenth century Pope Innocent X made it a showcase of Baroque Rome. At its centre, Gian Lorenzo Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers, completed in 1651, represents the Nile, the Ganges, the Danube and the Río de la Plata, crowned by an Egyptian-style obelisk. Facing it, the church of Sant'Agnese in Agone is by Bernini's great rival Borromini; legend says Bernini's statues shield their eyes from the church, though the fountain was finished first. Two smaller fountains, of the Moor and of Neptune, complete the square.
rom.trevi: The Trevi Fountain, completed in 1762 to designs by Nicola Salvi, marks the end of the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct built in 19 BC that still brings water to the centre of Rome. At 26 metres high and almost 50 metres wide, it is the largest Baroque fountain in the city. Oceanus, the god of water, rides a shell-shaped chariot pulled by two sea horses, one calm and one wild, symbolising the moods of the sea. Tradition says that throwing a coin over your left shoulder with your right hand ensures you will return to Rome; around 1.5 million euros are collected each year and given to charity. Anita Ekberg's scene in Fellini's La Dolce Vita made the fountain world-famous.
rom.spagna: The Spanish Steps, 135 steps built between 1723 and 1726, link the Piazza di Spagna below with the French church of Trinità dei Monti above; they were paid for by a French diplomat. The square takes its name from the Spanish Embassy to the Holy See, there since the seventeenth century. At the foot of the steps, the Barcaccia fountain, shaped like a sinking boat, is by Pietro Bernini, father of Gian Lorenzo. The house to the right is where the English poet John Keats died in 1821, now a museum dedicated to him and Shelley. From the square, Via dei Condotti is lined with luxury boutiques. Sitting on the steps is now forbidden, to protect them.
rom.sao-pedro-vat: St Peter's Square, designed by Gian Lorenzo Bernini between 1656 and 1667, is the entrance to the Vatican City, the smallest state in the world. Its two semicircular colonnades, with 284 columns and 140 statues of saints, symbolise the arms of the Church embracing the faithful. From one of the two discs in the pavement near the fountains, the four rows of columns align perfectly into one. At the centre stands an Egyptian obelisk brought to Rome by Emperor Caligula. St Peter's Basilica, built over the tomb of the apostle Peter, was completed in 1626, with a dome designed by Michelangelo. Entry to the basilica is free, but expect security queues and cover your shoulders and knees.

ams.centraal: Amsterdam Central Station was built on three artificial islands in the IJ waterway and opened in 1889. It was designed by Pierre Cuypers, also the architect of the Rijksmuseum, in a mix of Gothic and Renaissance styles, and rests on almost nine thousand wooden piles. Its construction cut the city off from its open waterfront, which caused controversy at the time. Behind the station, free ferries cross the IJ to Amsterdam Noord. In front, the Damrak was once a harbour inlet where ships unloaded their cargo; today it leads towards the centre. Look for the Beurs van Berlage, the old stock exchange of 1903, considered the start of modern Dutch architecture.
ams.dam: Dam Square marks the spot where the Amstel river was dammed around 1270, the origin of the city and its name, Amstelredam. The Royal Palace, built between 1648 and 1665 as the City Hall at the height of the Dutch Golden Age, rests on 13,659 wooden piles. It became a royal palace under Louis Bonaparte in 1808 and is still used by the King for state visits. Next to it, the Nieuwe Kerk, the New Church, from the fifteenth century, is where Dutch monarchs are inaugurated. Opposite, the white National Monument commemorates the victims of the Second World War. The square is also home to the Madame Tussauds wax museum and the department store De Bijenkorf.
ams.begijnhof: The Begijnhof is a hidden courtyard dating from the fourteenth century, one of the oldest in Amsterdam. It was home to the Beguines, a Catholic sisterhood of unmarried women who lived in community and devoted themselves to charity without taking vows. The last Beguine died in 1971, and women still live in the houses today. Around the quiet garden stand the English Reformed Church, used by English-speaking Protestants, and a clandestine Catholic chapel from the time when Catholic worship was banned. Number 34, the Houten Huys, built around 1528, is one of only two wooden houses left in the city centre. Please keep your voice down: this is a residential place.
ams.bloemenmarkt: The Bloemenmarkt on the Singel canal is said to be the only floating flower market in the world. It has existed since 1862, when growers sailed along the Amstel to sell their flowers directly from their boats. Today the stalls stand on permanent houseboats. It is the place to buy tulip bulbs, a Dutch passion since the seventeenth century, when the so-called tulip mania made a single rare bulb worth more than a canal house, one of the first speculative bubbles in history. Check that bulbs are certified for export if you plan to take them home. The Singel was the city's moat until the fifteenth century and is the innermost ring of the canal belt.
ams.nove-ruas: The Nine Streets are small cross streets connecting the Singel, Herengracht, Keizersgracht and Prinsengracht, four of the canals of the Golden Age canal ring, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2010. The canal belt was dug in the seventeenth century as a planned extension for wealthy merchants, whose tall, narrow houses have gabled façades and hooks at the top to hoist furniture through the windows, because the staircases are too steep. Houses were taxed by width, which explains their narrow fronts. The Nine Streets are full of independent boutiques, vintage shops, cheese shops and cafés. Stop on any bridge for one of the most photographed views of Amsterdam.
ams.anne-frank: At Prinsengracht 263, Anne Frank, her family and four other Jewish people hid from the Nazis for more than two years, from July 1942, in a secret annex behind a movable bookcase. They were betrayed and arrested in August 1944; Anne died in the Bergen-Belsen camp in early 1945, aged fifteen. Her diary, published by her father Otto, the only survivor, has been translated into more than seventy languages. The house is now a museum, and tickets must be booked online in advance. Next to it, the Westerkerk, completed in 1631, has the tallest church tower in Amsterdam; Anne mentioned its bells in her diary. The painter Rembrandt is buried there in an unknown grave.
ams.rijksmuseum: The Rijksmuseum is the national museum of the Netherlands, in a building by Pierre Cuypers that opened in 1885. A cycle path runs right through its central passage, a unique feature defended by Amsterdam's cyclists. Its star is Rembrandt's The Night Watch, painted in 1642, the subject of a major restoration visible to visitors. You will also see Vermeer's The Milkmaid and works by Frans Hals and Jan Steen, along with Delftware, dolls' houses and ship models from the Golden Age. In front, the Museumplein, a large lawn, connects the Rijksmuseum, the Van Gogh Museum and the Stedelijk modern art museum, with the Concertgebouw concert hall at the far end.
ams.vondelpark: The Vondelpark opened in 1865 and is Amsterdam's most popular park, with around ten million visitors a year. It is named after Joost van den Vondel, the seventeenth-century poet often called the Dutch Shakespeare, whose statue stands in the park. Designed in the English landscape style, it has winding paths, ponds, lawns and a rose garden. In the 1970s it became a famous gathering place for hippies who slept in the park. Today locals come to cycle, jog, picnic and, in summer, enjoy free concerts at the open-air theatre. Look for the tall Picasso sculpture called The Fish, donated by the artist in 1965, and the Blue Teahouse, a café from 1937.

edi.scott: Princes Street Gardens occupy the bed of the Nor Loch, a polluted lake drained in the nineteenth century that once protected the castle from the north. The gardens separate the medieval Old Town from the elegant Georgian New Town, built from the 1760s on a planned grid; together they form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Scott Monument, completed in 1846, honours the novelist Sir Walter Scott, author of Ivanhoe. At 61 metres it is the largest monument to a writer in the world, and its 287 steps lead to a narrow gallery at the top. Its blackened sandstone comes from decades of coal smoke. At the foot of the gardens you can see the floral clock, planted every year since 1903.
edi.calton: Calton Hill is one of Edinburgh's seven hills and offers the most famous panorama of the city. Its unfinished National Monument, begun in 1826 as a copy of the Parthenon to honour the Scottish dead of the Napoleonic Wars, ran out of money after twelve columns, earning it the nickname Edinburgh's Disgrace; its ruins helped give the city the name Athens of the North. The Nelson Monument, shaped like an upturned telescope, has a time ball that drops at 1 pm every day, once a signal for ships in the port of Leith. From the summit you see the castle, the Royal Mile, Arthur's Seat and the Firth of Forth. The Dugald Stewart Monument is the classic spot for photographs.
edi.st-giles: The Royal Mile is the chain of streets running downhill from Edinburgh Castle to the Palace of Holyroodhouse, along the spine of the old volcanic ridge. Tall stone tenements, some ten storeys high, line its sides, and narrow closes lead off to hidden courtyards. St Giles' Cathedral, with its distinctive crown spire from the fifteenth century, was the church of John Knox, leader of the Scottish Reformation in 1560. Inside, the Thistle Chapel, built in 1911 for Scotland's order of chivalry, is a jewel of carved wood. On the pavement outside, the Heart of Midlothian marks the site of the old prison; locals spit on it for luck. Further down, the Old Town still has the house of John Knox.
edi.castle: Edinburgh Castle stands on Castle Rock, the plug of an extinct volcano that has been fortified for at least three thousand years. It was besieged more times than almost any other place in Britain. The oldest building in the city, Saint Margaret's Chapel, dates from around 1130. Inside the castle you can see the Honours of Scotland, the oldest crown jewels in the British Isles, and the vaulted prisons where prisoners of war were held. Every day except Sunday, the One O'Clock Gun is fired from the battlements. In August, the esplanade hosts the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo, with bagpipe bands from around the world. The esplanade is free; the interior is paid.
edi.victoria-st: Victoria Street curves down from George IV Bridge to the Grassmarket. It was built in the 1830s to improve access to the Old Town, and its colourful shopfronts, with an elevated terrace above, are said to have inspired Diagon Alley in the Harry Potter books, whose author J. K. Rowling wrote in nearby cafés. The Grassmarket below was a market for horses and cattle from 1477 and also the site of public hangings; a memorial marks where Covenanters were executed in the seventeenth century. Today it is lined with pubs, such as the White Hart Inn, one of the oldest in the city, where the poet Robert Burns is said to have stayed. The castle rises dramatically above the square.
edi.nms: The National Museum of Scotland combines a Victorian building of 1866, with a spectacular glass-roofed Grand Gallery, and a modern sandstone extension of 1998 dedicated to Scottish history. Its collections range from geology and natural history to world cultures and science. Among its most famous objects are Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell in 1996, the Lewis Chessmen carved from walrus ivory in the twelfth century, and the Millennium Clock. Entry is free. Take the lift to the rooftop terrace for a superb view of the castle and the Old Town. Across the road, the statue of Greyfriars Bobby recalls the loyal dog said to have guarded his master's grave for fourteen years.
edi.holyrood: At the bottom of the Royal Mile, the Palace of Holyroodhouse is the official residence of the British monarch in Scotland. It grew from a twelfth-century abbey, whose ruins still stand beside it, and is famous as the home of Mary, Queen of Scots, whose secretary David Rizzio was murdered in front of her in 1566. Opposite, the Scottish Parliament building, opened in 2004 and designed by the Catalan architect Enric Miralles, is a striking piece of modern architecture. Behind rises Arthur's Seat, an extinct volcano 251 metres high in Holyrood Park. The path to Salisbury Crags gives sweeping views; the full climb to the summit takes about an hour return.

man.piccadilly-g: Piccadilly Gardens is the main square of Manchester city centre, laid out on the site of the Manchester Royal Infirmary, which stood here from 1755 to 1909. Statues of Queen Victoria, the Duke of Wellington and the engineer James Watt recall the industrial nineteenth century, when Manchester became the world's first industrial city, nicknamed Cottonopolis for its cotton mills. The square is the hub for trams and buses, including the free city-centre buses. The concrete wall by Japanese architect Tadao Ando, added in 2002, divides opinion among locals. From here, Market Street is the main shopping street, and the Northern Quarter lies just across the road.
man.nq: The Northern Quarter grew in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries around textile warehouses, markets and workshops. After decades of decline, it was revived from the 1980s by artists, record shops and independent businesses, and is now Manchester's creative heart. Its red-brick streets and iron fire escapes are so similar to old New York that they have doubled for it in Hollywood films. Look for the colourful murals and street art, especially around Stevenson Square, where the walls are repainted regularly. Afflecks, an indoor market of alternative fashion and curiosities since 1982, is an institution. The quarter is full of cafés, vintage shops and music venues linked to the city's famous music scene.
man.cathedral-m: Manchester Cathedral, mostly built in the fifteenth century in the Perpendicular Gothic style, has the widest nave of any cathedral in England and remarkable medieval wooden choir stalls with carved misericords. It was damaged by a German bomb in 1940 and again by the IRA bomb of 1996, which devastated the city centre and led to its regeneration. Next door, the striking glass building called Urbis houses the National Football Museum, which tells the story of the game in the city that is home to Manchester United and Manchester City. Nearby, Chetham's Library, founded in 1653, is the oldest public library in the English-speaking world, where Marx and Engels studied together.
man.rylands: The John Rylands Library was built by Enriqueta Rylands in memory of her husband John, Manchester's richest cotton merchant, and opened in 1900. Designed by Basil Champneys, its neo-Gothic reading room looks like a cathedral, with vaulted ceilings, stained-glass windows and statues of John and Enriqueta facing each other. It was one of the first buildings in Manchester lit by electricity. Now part of the University of Manchester, it holds rare treasures, including the Rylands Papyrus, the oldest known fragment of the New Testament, and a Gutenberg Bible. Entry is free. Around the corner, Deansgate is one of the main streets of the city, following the line of a Roman road.
man.albert-sq: Albert Square is named after Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's husband, whose memorial stands in the square. Its north side is dominated by Manchester Town Hall, a neo-Gothic masterpiece by Alfred Waterhouse completed in 1877, with an 85-metre clock tower and murals by Ford Madox Brown; it has been undergoing a major restoration. A few steps south, St Peter's Square is home to the Central Library, a circular domed building from 1934 inspired by the Pantheon in Rome. The square is also the site of the Peterloo Massacre of 1819, when cavalry charged a peaceful crowd demanding parliamentary reform, killing eighteen people; a memorial recalls the event.
man.castlefield: Castlefield is where Manchester began: the Romans built a fort called Mamucium here around 79 AD, and part of it has been reconstructed. In 1761 the Bridgewater Canal, considered the first canal of the Industrial Revolution, arrived here to bring coal from the Duke of Bridgewater's mines, and in 1830 the world's first passenger railway station, Liverpool Road, opened nearby. Today the station is part of the Science and Industry Museum. The basin, with its warehouses, iron railway viaducts and canal boats, became the first urban heritage park in Britain. It is a peaceful place to walk, with pubs and terraces along the water, a striking contrast to the busy city centre.
man.old-trafford: Old Trafford, nicknamed the Theatre of Dreams by Sir Bobby Charlton, has been the home of Manchester United since 1910. With around 74,000 seats it is the largest club stadium in Britain. The club rebuilt it after it was bombed in 1941. Outside the East Stand, the United Trinity statue depicts George Best, Denis Law and Bobby Charlton, and a clock stopped at the time of the Munich air disaster of 1958, in which eight players died, honours the Busby Babes. The museum and stadium tour let you see the dressing rooms and walk down the players' tunnel. Nearby, Old Trafford cricket ground is the home of Lancashire cricket, not to be confused with the football stadium.

gla.george-sq: George Square, laid out in 1781 and named after King George III, is Glasgow's civic heart. Ironically, the king himself is absent: the tall central column, erected in 1837, carries Sir Walter Scott, and the square is surrounded by statues of figures such as Robert Burns, James Watt and Queen Victoria on horseback. The east side is dominated by the City Chambers, opened in 1888 when Glasgow was the Second City of the British Empire, rich from tobacco, shipbuilding and trade. Its interior of marble staircases and mosaics can be seen on free guided tours when available. The square is the site of celebrations, protests and the Christmas market, and Queen Street station is right next to it.
gla.necropolis: Glasgow Cathedral, dedicated to Saint Mungo, the city's founder and patron saint, is the only medieval cathedral on mainland Scotland to have survived the Reformation of 1560 almost intact, because the city's trades defended it. Its present building dates mainly from the thirteenth century, and the crypt holds the tomb of Saint Mungo. Behind it, crossing the Bridge of Sighs, the Necropolis is a Victorian garden cemetery opened in 1833 on a hill, with around 3,500 monuments, including a column to John Knox and tombs designed by Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Alexander Thomson. Its summit offers one of the best views of the city. Across the street, Provand's Lordship, from 1471, is Glasgow's oldest house.
gla.merchant: The Merchant City was where the eighteenth-century Tobacco Lords, merchants who grew rich importing tobacco from the plantations of Virginia, built their mansions and warehouses. Many streets are named after them and the colonies, such as Virginia Street, and the area's history is linked to the Atlantic slave trade, which the city is now openly acknowledging. After decades of decline, the area was restored and is now full of restaurants, bars and boutiques. It is also the heart of the City Centre Mural Trail: huge murals painted on building walls, such as the portrait of Saint Mungo and the hyper-realistic works by Smug, have become one of Glasgow's most popular attractions.
gla.buchanan: Buchanan Street is Glasgow's main shopping street, pedestrianised and lined with Victorian buildings and modern malls. At its northern end, the statue of Donald Dewar, Scotland's first First Minister, stands in front of the Royal Concert Hall. Just off the street, in Mitchell Lane, The Lighthouse occupies the former offices of the Glasgow Herald newspaper, designed in 1895 by a young Charles Rennie Mackintosh, the city's most famous architect. It is now Scotland's Centre for Design and Architecture, and its spiral staircase leads to a viewing platform with a panorama over the rooftops. Nearby, the Willow Tea Rooms recreate the tea rooms Mackintosh designed in 1903 for Kate Cranston.
gla.kelvingrove: Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum opened in 1901 for the Glasgow International Exhibition and is one of the most visited museums in the United Kingdom, with free entry. Its red sandstone building in Spanish Baroque style houses 22 galleries with around 8,000 objects, from a Spitfire hanging from the ceiling to a stuffed elephant named Sir Roger. Its most famous painting is Salvador Dalí's Christ of Saint John of the Cross, bought by the city in 1952 amid controversy. There are also works by the Glasgow Boys, the Scottish Colourists and a gallery dedicated to Charles Rennie Mackintosh. Every day, a recital is played on the great concert organ in the central hall.
gla.uni-gla: The University of Glasgow, founded in 1451, is the fourth-oldest university in the English-speaking world. Its alumni include the economist Adam Smith, the engineer James Watt, the physicist Lord Kelvin and the father of antiseptic surgery, Joseph Lister. The university moved to its present site on Gilmorehill in 1870, to a Gothic Revival building by George Gilbert Scott, with a tower 85 metres high visible across the West End. Its vaulted Cloisters, with arched stone ribs and pillars, are among the most photographed places in the city and have appeared in films and series. The Hunterian Museum, the oldest public museum in Scotland, is located inside the main building.
gla.riverside: The Riverside Museum, Scotland's museum of transport and travel, opened in 2011 in a building designed by Zaha Hadid; its zigzag roof evokes the waves and the sheds of the shipyards that once lined the River Clyde. The Clyde built a fifth of the world's ships at its peak, including the Queen Mary and the Queen Elizabeth 2. Inside, free collections include old trams, steam locomotives, cars, bicycles and a reconstructed Glasgow street from the early twentieth century. Moored outside is the Glenlee, a three-masted sailing ship launched in 1896 that sailed around Cape Horn several times, one of only five Clyde-built sailing ships still afloat. It won the European Museum of the Year award in 2013.

liv.albert-dock: The Royal Albert Dock was opened in 1846 by Prince Albert and designed by Jesse Hartley. It was the first structure in Britain built entirely of cast iron, brick and stone, with no structural wood, so it was fireproof, and ships could unload directly into its warehouses. In the nineteenth century Liverpool was one of the busiest ports in the world, through which cotton, sugar and tobacco flowed, and from which millions of emigrants sailed for America; the port's wealth was also built on the transatlantic slave trade. The dock closed in 1972 and was restored in the 1980s. Today it houses Tate Liverpool, the Merseyside Maritime Museum and the International Slavery Museum.
liv.beatles-story: The Beatles Story, at the Royal Albert Dock, is one of the largest permanent exhibitions in the world dedicated to a single band. It traces the story of John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr, from their childhood in Liverpool and their first concerts to Beatlemania and their solo careers. It includes replicas of the Cavern Club, the Casbah Club and Abbey Road Studios, as well as original instruments and personal items, such as glasses worn by Lennon. The Beatles sold hundreds of millions of records and are considered the most influential band in history. Liverpool calls itself the World Capital City of Pop, with more number-one singles than any other city.
liv.pier-head: Pier Head is Liverpool's iconic waterfront, dominated by the Three Graces, three buildings from the early twentieth century that symbolised the city's wealth as a great port. The Royal Liver Building, completed in 1911, was one of the first large buildings made of reinforced concrete; its two towers carry the Liver Birds, mythical birds that are the symbol of the city. Legend says that if they ever fly away, Liverpool will cease to exist. Next to it stand the Cunard Building, the former headquarters of the Cunard Line, owner of liners such as the Lusitania and the Queen Mary, and the domed Port of Liverpool Building. On the promenade, the bronze statue of the four Beatles has been a favourite photo spot since 2015.
liv.museum-liv: The Museum of Liverpool opened in 2011 in a striking white building on the waterfront and was the first national museum devoted to the history of a city. It won the European Museum of the Year award in 2013. Its galleries tell the story of Liverpool from prehistoric times to the present: its role as a global port, the arrival of Irish, Welsh, Chinese and Caribbean communities, the city's musical heritage and its football rivalry between Liverpool and Everton. You can also see the Lion locomotive from 1838, one of the oldest working engines in the world. Entry is free, and the large windows offer views over the River Mersey and the Three Graces.
liv.cavern: Mathew Street is the narrow street where the Cavern Club opened in 1957 as a jazz club in an old fruit warehouse cellar. The Beatles played there almost 300 times between 1961 and 1963, and it was in the Cavern that their future manager Brian Epstein first saw them in November 1961. The original club was demolished in 1973 for a railway project; the present club was rebuilt in 1984 using many of the original bricks, and live music is played there almost all day. In the street you will find a statue of John Lennon leaning against the wall, the Cavern Wall of Fame with the names of artists who played there, and pubs such as The Grapes, where the Beatles drank.
liv.st-georges: St George's Hall, opened in 1854, is considered one of the finest neoclassical buildings in the world. It was designed by Harvey Lonsdale Elmes, who won a competition at the age of 25 but died before it was finished. It combined a concert hall and law courts under one roof. Its Great Hall has a floor of more than 30,000 Minton tiles, usually covered to protect it and revealed only a few times a year, and one of the largest pipe organs in Britain. On the plateau in front, equestrian statues of Queen Victoria and Prince Albert overlook Lime Street station. The surrounding area, with the World Museum, the Walker Art Gallery and the Central Library, forms Liverpool's cultural quarter.
liv.met-cathedral: The Metropolitan Cathedral of Christ the King is Liverpool's Catholic cathedral. In 1933, construction began on a gigantic design by Sir Edwin Lutyens, which would have had the second-largest dome in the world, but the Second World War stopped the work; only the crypt was completed. The present building, designed by Frederick Gibberd and consecrated in 1967, is circular, so that the congregation surrounds the altar. Locals nicknamed it Paddy's Wigwam because of its tent-like shape. Its central lantern of stained glass by John Piper and Patrick Reyntiens bathes the interior in blue, red and yellow light. Hope Street connects it to the Anglican cathedral, symbolising the friendship of the two churches.
liv.liv-cathedral: Liverpool Cathedral, the Anglican cathedral, is the largest cathedral and religious building in Britain and one of the largest in the world. It was designed by Giles Gilbert Scott, who won the competition in 1903 at only 22 and was a Catholic. Construction began in 1904 and was only completed in 1978, eighteen years after his death. Its tower, 101 metres high, houses the highest and heaviest ring of bells in the world. Inside, the nave is vast and the stained-glass windows include images of everyday life. A lift and stairs take visitors to the top of the tower, with a view as far as Wales. At its feet, Hope Street is lined with restaurants and the Liverpool Philharmonic hall.

bir.bullring: The Bullring has been Birmingham's market place since the twelfth century, when the lord of the manor obtained a royal charter for a market in 1166; the name comes from the ring where bulls were tied before slaughter. The current shopping centre, opened in 2003, is famous for the Selfridges building, a curved shell covered with 15,000 shiny aluminium discs, inspired by a sequinned dress. Beside it, St Martin in the Bull Ring, the city's parish church, was rebuilt in 1873 on medieval foundations and has a stained-glass window by Edward Burne-Jones, a native of Birmingham. A bronze bull sculpture by Laurence Broderick, a favourite meeting point, stands at the entrance. The open-air market continues nearby.
bir.victoria-sq: Victoria Square is Birmingham's civic centre. The Town Hall, completed in 1834 and modelled on a Roman temple, is a concert hall where Mendelssohn conducted the premiere of his oratorio Elijah in 1846; Charles Dickens gave readings here too. Next to it, the Council House, from 1879, has a clock tower nicknamed Big Brum. In the centre, the reclining female figure of The River is known locally as the Floozie in the Jacuzzi, and a statue of Queen Victoria completes the square. Birmingham grew from a small market town into the workshop of the world during the Industrial Revolution, with thousands of trades, earning it the title City of a Thousand Trades.
bir.library-b: The Library of Birmingham, opened in 2013 and designed by the Dutch firm Mecanoo, is one of the largest public libraries in Europe. Its façade is wrapped in interlocking metal rings that recall the city's jewellery and metalworking traditions. Escalators rise through the building past circular rotundas of books to the outdoor terraces, with gardens and views over the city, and to the Shakespeare Memorial Room, a Victorian reading room moved here from the old library. Its collections include one of the most important Shakespeare collections in the world. Outside, Centenary Square features a monument to Boulton, Watt and Murdoch, the pioneers of the steam engine, nicknamed the Golden Boys.
bir.gas-street: Birmingham is often said to have more miles of canals than Venice, with about 35 miles in the city and around 100 across the region. The canals were dug from the 1760s to carry coal and goods during the Industrial Revolution, linking the city to the rest of England. Gas Street Basin, the heart of the network, was named after the gas lamps that lit the street in the early nineteenth century. Today, colourful narrowboats moor among restored warehouses, pubs and restaurants. A short walk leads to Brindleyplace, named after the canal engineer James Brindley, with squares, cafés and the Ikon contemporary art gallery in a neo-Gothic former school. Towpaths make for an easy, flat walk.
bir.jq: The Jewellery Quarter has been a centre of jewellery-making for more than 250 years, and still produces a large share of the jewellery made in Britain; it has hundreds of workshops and shops. The Birmingham Assay Office, founded in 1773, still hallmarks precious metals with its anchor symbol. At the central crossroads stands the Chamberlain Clock, from 1903, honouring the politician Joseph Chamberlain. The Museum of the Jewellery Quarter preserves the Smith and Pepper workshop exactly as it was when it closed in 1981. The quarter also contains the Pen Museum, since Birmingham once made most of the world's steel pen nibs, and two historic cemeteries, Key Hill and Warstone Lane.
bir.cadbury: Bournville is the model village built by the Cadbury brothers, George and Richard, Quaker chocolate makers who moved their factory out of the industrial city in 1879 to a greener site. They built houses with gardens, parks and sports grounds for their workers, an early example of a planned garden village; following Quaker principles, no pubs were allowed. Cadbury World, the visitor attraction next to the factory, tells the history of chocolate from the Aztecs to the creation of the Dairy Milk bar in 1905, with demonstrations and tastings. Booking ahead is recommended. The village green, the Carillon with its 48 bells and the half-timbered Selly Manor museum are worth a stroll.

ist.taksim: Taksim Square is the heart of modern Istanbul, on the European side. Its name means distribution, after the stone reservoir built in the 1730s that distributed water from the northern forests to the city; the octagonal building still stands at the edge of the square. At the centre, the Republic Monument, unveiled in 1928, shows Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and the founders of the Turkish Republic. The square has long been the stage for celebrations and political demonstrations. On its north side, the Taksim Mosque, opened in 2021, and the Atatürk Cultural Center, rebuilt in 2021, face each other. From here, İstiklal Avenue leads down towards Galata, and the historic red tram departs.
ist.istiklal: İstiklal Avenue, whose name means Independence, is a pedestrian street about 1.4 kilometres long, once called the Grande Rue de Péra. In the nineteenth century this was the most European quarter of the Ottoman capital, home to embassies, Levantine merchants, theatres and cafés. Its Art Nouveau and neoclassical buildings house shops, bookshops and cinemas. Look for the arcades: Çiçek Pasajı, the Flower Passage, with its old meyhane taverns, and the Hazzopulo passage. Halfway down stand the Catholic church of Saint Anthony of Padua and the Galatasaray High School, founded in 1481. The nostalgic red tram has run along the avenue since 1990, recalling the trams of the early twentieth century.
ist.galata: The Galata Tower was built by the Genoese in 1348, when Galata was a Genoese colony facing Byzantine Constantinople, and at 67 metres it was then the tallest building in the city. The Ottomans used it as a prison, an observatory and a fire lookout tower. Legend says that in the seventeenth century Hezarfen Ahmed Çelebi flew from its top with artificial wings across the Bosphorus to Üsküdar. A circular balcony at the top offers a 360-degree view of the Golden Horn, the old city and the Bosphorus; the visit is paid, and it is best to arrive early. The surrounding streets of Karaköy and Galata are full of cafés, design shops and staircases, such as the Camondo Stairs.
ist.galata-bridge: The Galata Bridge crosses the Golden Horn, the natural harbour that separates the old city from Galata and Beyoğlu. The first bridge here was built in 1845; Leonardo da Vinci had already proposed a single-span design to Sultan Bayezid II in 1502, which was never built. The present bridge, the fifth, opened in 1994. On its upper deck, dozens of anglers line the railings day and night, and on the lower deck, fish restaurants and cafés face the water. From the bridge you see the silhouette of the old city: the New Mosque, the Süleymaniye Mosque on its hill and the domes of Topkapı. At Eminönü, at its southern end, boats grill fish to make the famous balık ekmek.
ist.spice: The Spice Bazaar, or Mısır Çarşısı, the Egyptian Bazaar, was completed in 1664 as part of the New Mosque complex; its rents paid for the upkeep of the mosque. Its name comes from the goods that arrived from Egypt, especially spices, which made it the centre of the spice trade in Istanbul. Its L-shaped vaulted hall houses about 85 shops selling spices, dried fruits, teas, Turkish delight, nuts, saffron and caviar. Tasting is usually free, and the prices are clearly displayed. Next door, the New Mosque, Yeni Cami, was begun in 1597 by the mother of Sultan Mehmed III and completed in 1665. Around the bazaar, the narrow streets of Eminönü are filled with shops selling coffee and cheeses.
ist.hagia-sophia: Hagia Sophia, the Church of Holy Wisdom, was built in just five years under Emperor Justinian and consecrated in 537. Its dome, 31 metres in diameter and seeming to float on a ring of windows, was the largest in the world for almost a thousand years. It was the cathedral of Constantinople for nine centuries, where Byzantine emperors were crowned. After the Ottoman conquest in 1453, Sultan Mehmed II turned it into a mosque and minarets were added. In 1934 Atatürk made it a museum, and in 2020 it became a mosque again. Byzantine mosaics of Christ, the Virgin Mary and emperors can still be seen in the galleries. Foreign visitors enter the upper gallery with a paid ticket.
ist.blue-mosque: The Sultan Ahmed Mosque, known as the Blue Mosque for the more than 20,000 blue İznik tiles that decorate its interior, was built between 1609 and 1616 by the young Sultan Ahmed I, facing Hagia Sophia. It was the first mosque in Istanbul with six minarets, which caused controversy at the time because only the mosque in Mecca had as many. Its cascade of domes and semi-domes is one of the masterpieces of classical Ottoman architecture. Entry is free outside prayer times; shoes must be removed and shoulders and knees covered. In front, the Hippodrome was the centre of Byzantine Constantinople, where chariot races took place; the Egyptian obelisk and the bronze Serpent Column still stand.
ist.cistern: The Basilica Cistern, or Yerebatan Sarayı, the Sunken Palace, was built in 532 under Emperor Justinian to store water for the Great Palace and the buildings around it. It could hold about 80,000 cubic metres of water, brought by aqueducts from the forests north of the city. Its roof is supported by 336 marble columns, 9 metres high, many of them taken from older buildings. In the north-west corner, two columns rest on carved heads of Medusa, one upside down and one on its side, whose origin is unknown. The cistern was forgotten for centuries until it was rediscovered in the sixteenth century. It appeared in the James Bond film From Russia with Love and in Dan Brown's novel Inferno.
ist.grand-bazaar: The Grand Bazaar, Kapalıçarşı, the Covered Market, is one of the largest and oldest covered markets in the world. Its core was built by Sultan Mehmed II shortly after the conquest of 1453, and it grew into a labyrinth of more than 60 covered streets and around 4,000 shops, with mosques, fountains, cafés and inns called hans, where merchants once lodged with their goods. Here you will find carpets, jewellery, ceramics, leather, lamps and textiles. Bargaining is part of the experience: take your time, compare prices and enjoy the tea offered by the shopkeepers. The bazaar is closed on Sundays. Near the Beyazıt Gate, the second-hand book market of Sahaflar has existed since Byzantine times.
ist.topkapi: Topkapı Palace was the residence and seat of government of the Ottoman sultans for almost four centuries, from the 1460s until 1856, when they moved to Dolmabahçe. Built by Mehmed II on the tip of the historic peninsula, it is a series of courtyards and pavilions rather than a single building, with views of the Bosphorus, the Golden Horn and the Sea of Marmara. Its treasures include the Topkapı Dagger, the Spoonmaker's Diamond, one of the largest in the world, and sacred relics of the Prophet Muhammad. The Harem, with more than 300 rooms richly decorated with tiles, was the private residence of the sultan's family. The palace has been a museum since 1924 and is closed on Tuesdays.
ist.uskudar: The ferry from Eminönü to Üsküdar crosses the Bosphorus, the strait that separates Europe from Asia, in about twenty minutes, for the price of a single transport ticket. From the deck you see the old city, Topkapı Palace and the Galata Tower, while seagulls follow the boat. Üsküdar, on the Asian side, is one of the oldest districts of Istanbul, a conservative and lively neighbourhood with beautiful Ottoman mosques, such as the Mihrimah Sultan Mosque by the great architect Mimar Sinan, right on the square by the pier. Along the shore, cafés face the Maiden's Tower, a lighthouse on a small islet whose history goes back to Byzantine times, reopened in 2023 after restoration. Sunset here is unforgettable.

dxb.al-fahidi: Al Fahidi, long known as Al Bastakiya, is one of the few corners of Dubai that predates oil. In the late 19th century merchants from the Persian coast settled here and built houses of coral stone, gypsum and palm wood around shaded courtyards. Above the roofs rise the barjeel, wind towers that catch the breeze and push it down into the rooms, a clever form of air conditioning long before electricity. Today the narrow lanes hold small galleries, the Coffee Museum, craft shops and cafés serving cardamom tea. Nearby, the Al Fahidi Fort, built around 1787, is the oldest building in the city.
dxb.abra: For centuries Dubai Creek was the city's highway and its reason to exist: pearl divers, dhows from India and Iran, and traders all met on this saltwater inlet. The abra, a small wooden water taxi, still links Bur Dubai and Deira for one dirham, paid in cash to the boatman. The crossing takes a few minutes and is one of the best views of old Dubai, with dhows unloading cargo along the wharves. On the Deira side the Spice Souk fills the alleys with sacks of saffron, frankincense, dried lemons, cardamom and rose petals. Sellers will call you in; looking is free and bargaining is expected.
dxb.gold-souk: A few minutes' walk from the spice market, Dubai's Gold Souk gathers several hundred shops in a covered arcade, their windows packed with necklaces, bangles and bridal sets. Gold is sold by weight at a price fixed daily by the market, with a separate charge for the craftsmanship, which is where bargaining happens. Purity is strictly controlled by the authorities, so 18, 21, 22 and 24 carat pieces are reliably what they claim. Even if you buy nothing, the sheer quantity is a spectacle. The souk is busiest in the evening, when the lights make the windows shine.
dxb.museum-future: Opened in 2022, the Museum of the Future is one of the most photographed buildings in the world: a silver torus with an empty centre, standing on a green mound beside Sheikh Zayed Road. Its stainless-steel skin is cut with Arabic calligraphy by the Emirati artist Mattar bin Lahej, quoting verses by the ruler of Dubai about the future. The calligraphy doubles as the building's windows. Inside, exhibitions imagine life in 2071 through immersive rooms on space, climate and health. Entry requires a timed ticket, but the outside, best at dusk when the letters glow, is free to admire.
dxb.burj-khalifa: At 828 metres, the Burj Khalifa has been the world's tallest building since it opened in 2010. Its Y-shaped plan was inspired by the desert flower Hymenocallis, and its setbacks spiral upwards to confuse the wind. Observation decks on levels 124, 125 and 148 look out over the city, the desert and the Gulf. At its feet the Dubai Mall is one of the largest malls on Earth, with an aquarium, an ice rink and hundreds of shops. In the evening the Dubai Fountain, on the lake between the tower and Souk Al Bahar, dances to music every half hour. The shows are free.
dxb.marina: Dubai Marina is an artificial canal three kilometres long, dug out of the desert in the early 2000s and lined with dozens of residential towers. The promenade, known as the Marina Walk, is ideal for an evening stroll among yachts, cafés and restaurants. Next to it, The Walk at JBR leads to a wide public beach with fine sand and warm, calm water, framed by the Ain Dubai observation wheel on Bluewaters Island. The Dubai Tram links the area to the metro. Come at sunset, when the towers light up and the heat finally eases.

auh.grand-mosque: The Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque, completed in 2007, was the dream of the founder of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, who is buried beside it. Builders and artists from many countries worked on it, combining Moorish, Mughal and Ottoman styles. It has 82 white domes, four minarets over 100 metres tall, and reflective pools that double the arches at night. Inside lies one of the world's largest hand-knotted carpets, made by around 1,200 weavers in Iran, under German crystal chandeliers. Entry is free with an online booking, and modest dress is required.
auh.qasr-watan: Qasr Al Watan, the Palace of the Nation, is a working presidential palace that opened its doors to visitors in 2019. Built of white granite and limestone, it hosts state visits and meetings of the Federal Supreme Council. The Great Hall sits beneath a dome 37 metres in diameter, one of the largest in the world, decorated with intricate gilded patterns. Exhibitions explain Arab contributions to science, astronomy and the arts, and the House of Knowledge library holds rare manuscripts. In the evening a sound and light show is projected onto the façade.
