auh.emirates-palace: Emirates Palace opened in 2005 as one of the most expensive hotels ever built, with more than a hundred domes, gold leaf on the ceilings and a private beach over a kilometre long. Now run as Emirates Palace Mandarin Oriental, it remains a symbol of Abu Dhabi's ambition, and its café is famous for cappuccino sprinkled with gold flakes. Across the road the five curved Etihad Towers rise above the sea; one of them hosts the Observation Deck at 300, the highest viewpoint in the capital, with views along the Corniche and over the islands.
auh.heritage-village: The Heritage Village, on the Breakwater opposite the Corniche, recreates life in the Emirates before oil. Palm-frond houses, a Bedouin tent, a small fort and a traditional falaj irrigation channel show how people survived the desert and the sea. Craftspeople demonstrate weaving, pottery and glass-blowing, and a tiny souk sells spices and handicrafts. Exhibits recall pearl diving, which was the region's main income until the 1930s. From the waterfront you get one of the best views of the city's skyline across the water. Entry is free.
auh.corniche-auh: The Corniche is Abu Dhabi's eight-kilometre waterfront, a landscaped promenade with cycle paths, palm-shaded gardens, fountains and a Blue Flag public beach. Until the 1960s the shoreline was little more than sand and fishermen's huts; the boulevard was built as the city grew rapidly with oil. Today families come here in the late afternoon when the temperature drops, to picnic, swim or ride shared bikes. The view of the skyline over the turquoise Gulf is one of the classic images of the capital, especially at sunset.
auh.louvre-auh: Louvre Abu Dhabi, designed by Jean Nouvel and opened in 2017, was born of an agreement between the UAE and France that lends it the Louvre name and loans from French museums. Its great dome, 180 metres wide, is made of eight layers of steel and aluminium forming nearly 8,000 star-shaped openings, so sunlight falls through in a shifting rain of light. Beneath it, the galleries are arranged like a small Arab town of white cubes on the sea. The collection tells human history chronologically, placing works from different civilisations side by side.

doh.msheireb: Msheireb Downtown Doha replaced one of the oldest quarters of the city with a new district designed around traditional Qatari architecture: narrow shaded streets, courtyards, light-coloured walls and wind-catching forms adapted to modern sustainable building. At its heart, four restored historic houses form the Msheireb Museums. Bin Jelmood House tells the story of slavery in the Indian Ocean, Company House the early oil workers, Mohammed bin Jassim House the history of the neighbourhood, and Radwani House everyday family life. Entry to the museums is free.
doh.souq-waqif: Souq Waqif has been Doha's trading place for over a century, where Bedouin brought livestock and goods to sell beside the Musheireb wadi. Rebuilt in 2006 with mud-rendered walls and wooden beams, it again feels like a traditional market. Alleys sell spices, perfumes, textiles, pottery and pets, and the Falcon Souq next door has shops of hooded falcons and a dedicated falcon hospital. Mounted police patrol on Arabian horses. In the evening the restaurants and shisha cafés fill with families, and the whole souq glows with lanterns.
doh.nmoq: The National Museum of Qatar, designed by Jean Nouvel and opened in 2019, takes the shape of a desert rose, the crystal formation found in the salt flats of the Gulf. Its hundreds of interlocking discs wrap around the restored palace of Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim Al Thani, which once served as the seat of government and the first national museum. Inside, a winding journey leads from the geology of the peninsula through Bedouin life and pearl diving to the discovery of oil and modern Qatar, using films projected on curved walls.
doh.mia: The Museum of Islamic Art was the last major work of the architect I. M. Pei, who came out of retirement and travelled the Islamic world for inspiration, settling on the ablution fountain of the Ibn Tulun Mosque in Cairo. Opened in 2008 on its own artificial island, the building rises in pale limestone cubes towards a central dome. It holds one of the world's finest collections of Islamic art, spanning 1,400 years from Spain to India: manuscripts, ceramics, metalwork and textiles. The surrounding MIA Park offers the best view of the West Bay towers.
doh.corniche-doh: Doha's Corniche curves for about seven kilometres around the bay, from the Museum of Islamic Art to the towers of West Bay. It was built in the 1970s on reclaimed land, giving the growing city a seafront promenade. Along the water, traditional wooden dhows wait for passengers and offer short cruises around the bay, especially beautiful at sunset. Look out for the giant pearl sculpture recalling the oyster divers who were the backbone of the local economy before oil. In the cooler months the promenade fills with runners, cyclists and families.
doh.katara: Katara Cultural Village, opened in 2010, was built to bring together Qatar's art and cultural institutions in one seaside district. Its Greek-style amphitheatre hosts concerts and festivals, and the opera house is home to the Qatar Philharmonic Orchestra. Look for the Blue Mosque covered in Persian-style tiles, the Golden Mosque, and the curious pigeon towers, inspired by traditional dovecotes. There are galleries, a public beach with water sports and restaurants of many cuisines. Katara's traditional dhow festival is held here each year.

ruh.kafd: The King Abdullah Financial District is one of Riyadh's most ambitious modern projects: a cluster of more than fifty towers designed to be the business heart of the kingdom. Its centrepiece for visitors is the metro station designed by Zaha Hadid Architects, a sculptural building whose undulating façade and luminous interior echo patterns formed by wind on desert sand. The station is a major interchange of the Riyadh Metro, which opened in late 2024 with six lines. Shaded walkways and air-conditioned skybridges connect the towers.
ruh.kingdom: The Kingdom Centre, completed in 2002, was one of the first great symbols of modern Riyadh. Its 302-metre silhouette ends in a parabolic arch with an empty space at the top, crossed by the Sky Bridge, a steel walkway about 300 metres above the street. A high-speed lift takes visitors up for one of the best views of the city: the grid of avenues, King Fahd Road and, on clear days, the desert beyond. At its base, a shopping mall includes a floor once reserved for women. At night the arch is lit in changing colours.
ruh.masmak: Al Masmak Fortress is where modern Saudi Arabia began. Built around 1865 of mud brick with thick walls and corner watchtowers, it was captured in a daring night raid in January 1902 by the young Abdulaziz bin Abdulrahman Al Saud, later the kingdom's founder. The spearhead lodged in its wooden door is still shown. Today the fortress is a museum with photographs, weapons and models telling the story of the unification. It stands beside Deira Square in the Qasr Al Hukm district, next to the Souq Al Zal with its rugs, incense and antiques.
ruh.national-museum-ruh: The National Museum of Saudi Arabia, opened in 1999 for the kingdom's centenary, is the largest museum in the country. Its curved façade evokes a desert dune. Eight halls follow the history of the Arabian Peninsula from the formation of the earth and the first rock art to the ancient kingdoms of the incense trade, the rise of Islam and the unification of the modern state. Highlights include stone stelae from Tayma, models of Mecca and Medina and artefacts from the pilgrim routes. It stands in the gardens of the King Abdulaziz Historical Center.
ruh.murabba: The Murabba Palace was built in the 1930s by King Abdulaziz outside the old city walls, when he moved his court from the cramped Masmak area. Its name means square, after the shape of the main building. Made of mud brick, straw and palm trunks, it shows how traditional Najdi architecture was adapted to a royal residence, with cool inner courtyards, carved wooden doors and triangular openings for ventilation. The rooms display the king's furniture, cars and personal objects. The palace stands within the same park as the National Museum, so the two make an easy pair.
ruh.diriyah: Diriyah, on the edge of the Wadi Hanifah valley, was the first capital of the Saudi state, founded in the 18th century. The At-Turaif district, with its mud-brick palaces and mosques, was destroyed by an Ottoman-Egyptian army in 1818 and left in ruins for nearly two centuries. In 2010 it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and it has since been restored with museums and night-time lighting. Across the valley, the Bujairi Terrace offers restaurants and cafés overlooking the ruins. The whole area is part of a vast development to become a cultural destination.

jed.al-balad: Al-Balad is the historic heart of Jeddah, founded as a fishing village and transformed in the 7th century into the port of Mecca. For centuries pilgrims from Africa and Asia landed here, and merchants grew rich on the trade. Their tower houses, built of coral stone from the Red Sea, rise four or five storeys and are famous for the rawasheen, large carved wooden bay windows that let air circulate while preserving privacy. The area became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. Nassif House, where King Abdulaziz stayed in 1925, now shows the interior of one of these homes.
jed.souq-alawi: Souq Al Alawi is the oldest and longest market street in Al-Balad, running roughly north to south through the historic town towards the old Makkah Gate, the route once taken by pilgrims heading to Mecca. Today it is still a lively place to shop for perfumes, oud and incense, dates, spices, fabrics, prayer beads and gold. Small side alleys open onto tiny squares and old mosques. The souq is busiest in the evening after the last prayer, when the heat eases and families come to stroll, buy sweets and drink tea at street stalls.
jed.matbouli: Matbouli House is a family home in Al-Balad converted into a museum by the descendants of the merchant who lived there. Built of coral stone and timber more than a century ago, it keeps its original layout across several floors, with reception rooms for men, private family quarters and a cool roof terrace. Each room is filled with everyday objects: furniture, kitchenware, clothes, radios, photographs and letters. Together they give a vivid picture of how a prosperous Jeddah household lived before the oil boom transformed the city.
jed.corniche-jed: The Jeddah Corniche runs for about thirty kilometres along the Red Sea, with promenades, beaches, playgrounds and fishing piers. In the 1970s and 1980s the city commissioned hundreds of open-air sculptures to decorate its roundabouts and seafront, including works by Henry Moore, Joan Miró, Alexander Calder and Arnaldo Pomodoro, making Jeddah one of the largest open-air museums in the world. Offshore, King Fahd's Fountain shoots seawater up to about 260 metres, the highest fountain in the world. It is lit up at night and visible from much of the city.
jed.al-rahma: Al Rahma Mosque, built in 1985 on stilts over the Red Sea, is known as the floating mosque because at high tide it seems to rest on the water. Its white walls and turquoise dome stand out against the blue sea, and windows on every side frame the horizon. The mosque mixes modern design with traditional Islamic architecture and is one of the most photographed sights of the northern Corniche. Non-Muslim visitors can usually admire it from the outside and the promenade; avoid prayer times and dress modestly if you approach the entrance.

cai.gem: The Grand Egyptian Museum, on the edge of the Giza plateau, is the largest museum in the world dedicated to a single civilisation. After two decades of construction it fully opened in 2025. Visitors are greeted in the atrium by a colossal 3,200-year-old granite statue of Ramesses II, moved here from central Cairo, before climbing a grand staircase lined with pharaohs and gods towards windows framing the pyramids. For the first time, the entire treasure of Tutankhamun, more than 5,000 objects including his gold mask and chariots, is shown together. The solar boat of Khufu is also displayed here.
cai.pyramids: The Pyramids of Giza were built around 4,500 years ago as tombs for three pharaohs of the Fourth Dynasty: Khufu, his son Khafre and Menkaure. The Great Pyramid of Khufu, originally 146 metres high, was the tallest structure made by humans for nearly four thousand years and is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. It contains about 2.3 million stone blocks. Archaeologists now know the builders were paid workers who lived in a nearby town. Go early to avoid heat and crowds; the panorama viewpoint gives the classic view of all nine pyramids.
cai.sphinx: The Great Sphinx was carved directly out of the limestone bedrock of the Giza plateau, most likely for the pharaoh Khafre around 2500 BC. With the body of a lion and a royal human head, it measures 73 metres long and 20 metres high, the largest monolithic statue in the ancient world. Its nose has been missing for centuries. Between its paws stands the Dream Stele of Thutmose IV, who cleared it from the sand after the Sphinx promised him the throne in a dream. The nearby Valley Temple of Khafre, built of huge granite blocks, frames the classic photo.
cai.egyptian-museum: The Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square opened in 1902 in a neoclassical pink building and for over a century was the world's main showcase of ancient Egypt. Even after many treasures moved to the new Grand Egyptian Museum, it still holds an extraordinary collection: colossal statues, painted coffins, the Narmer Palette that records Egypt's unification, the treasures of Yuya and Tjuyu and the Fayum mummy portraits. The crowded, old-fashioned display cases are part of its charm. Tahrir Square itself was the centre of the 2011 revolution.
cai.khan: Khan el-Khalili was founded in 1382 as a caravanserai for merchants in the heart of Fatimid Cairo, and it has been a market ever since. Its maze of alleys sells lanterns, copper, spices, perfumes, silver and textiles; bargaining is part of the experience. In a corner, El Fishawy café has served mint tea for more than two centuries. Just beside it runs Al-Muizz Street, one of the greatest concentrations of medieval Islamic architecture in the world, lined with mosques, madrasas, mausoleums and fountains from the Fatimid, Mamluk and Ottoman eras.
cai.citadel-cai: The Citadel was begun by Saladin in 1176 to defend Cairo against the Crusaders, and for nearly seven hundred years it was the seat of Egypt's rulers. Its skyline is dominated by the Mosque of Muhammad Ali, built between 1830 and 1848 in Ottoman style, with slender pencil minarets and walls clad in alabaster, which is why it is also called the Alabaster Mosque. Its courtyard has a clock tower given by King Louis-Philippe of France. From the terraces the view stretches over the minarets of Islamic Cairo and, on clear days, to the pyramids.

amm.citadel: The Amman Citadel, on Jabal al-Qal'a, is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places in the world, with traces of occupation from the Bronze Age. The Romans built the Temple of Hercules here in the 2nd century; two giant columns and the fingers of a colossal statue remain. Nearby stand a Byzantine church and the Umayyad Palace, an 8th-century complex with a restored domed audience hall. The Jordan Archaeological Museum displays finds from across the country. From the ramparts you see the whole of downtown Amman and the Roman Theatre below.
amm.roman-theatre: The Roman Theatre was built in the 2nd century during the reign of Antoninus Pius, when Amman was the city of Philadelphia, part of the Decapolis. Carved into the hillside and facing north to keep the sun out of spectators' eyes, it could seat about 6,000 people in three tiers. The acoustics are still remarkable: a word spoken in the centre carries to the top rows. The theatre is used again for concerts and festivals. Small museums in its wings show traditional costumes and folklore, and the smaller Odeon and the Nymphaeum stand nearby.
amm.downtown-amm: Downtown Amman, known as Al-Balad, lies in the valley where the Roman city once stood, below the hills where the modern city spread in the 20th century. It is the most traditional part of the capital: a dense web of streets lined with the gold souk, spice and coffee sellers, fruit stalls and shops of everything. The King Hussein Mosque, rebuilt in 1924 on the site of an older mosque, marks the centre. Hashem restaurant has served falafel and hummus around the clock for decades, and Habibah sweets sells the city's favourite knafeh.
amm.rainbow: Rainbow Street, officially Abu Bakr al-Siddiq Street, runs along Jabal Amman, one of the first residential hills of the modern city in the 1920s and 1930s. Its old stone villas, built by prominent families, now hold cafés, rooftop bars, bookshops and craft stores. The street is named after the old Rainbow Cinema. It is especially lively in the evening, when young Ammanis gather on terraces looking over the city lights. In summer the Souk Jara street market brings food stalls and crafts to the area on Fridays. It is close to the First Circle.
amm.abdullah-mosque: The King Abdullah I Mosque, completed in 1989, was built by King Hussein in memory of his grandfather, the founder of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. Its great dome, covered in blue mosaic tiles inscribed with verses from the Quran, is 35 metres wide and can be seen from much of the city. The octagonal prayer hall holds around 3,000 worshippers. It is one of the few mosques in Amman open to non-Muslim visitors outside prayer times; women are lent a cloak and headscarf at the entrance. A small Islamic museum is housed inside.

mct.grand-mosque-mct: The Sultan Qaboos Grand Mosque, opened in 2001, was a gift from Sultan Qaboos to the nation to mark 30 years of his reign. It is built of around 300,000 tonnes of Indian sandstone and has five minarets, symbolising the five pillars of Islam. The main prayer hall holds a vast Persian carpet woven in one piece by about 600 women over four years, and a Swarovski crystal chandelier 14 metres high. The marble corridors, gardens and arches show influences from across the Islamic world. Non-Muslim visitors are welcome in the morning with modest dress.
mct.opera-mct: The Royal Opera House Muscat, opened in 2011, was the first opera house in the Arabian Gulf and reflects Sultan Qaboos's passion for classical music. Built of pale desert limestone, it blends Omani palace architecture with Islamic geometric details, and its auditorium is lined with teak wood and can change shape for opera, concerts or theatre. Each seat has a screen with subtitles. The programme brings international orchestras, opera and ballet companies alongside Arab music. Gardens and a shopping gallery surround the building; guided tours run on certain days.
mct.mutrah: Mutrah grew up around a natural harbour between rocky mountains and the sea and was for centuries Muscat's commercial port. Its Corniche curves along the bay past old merchant houses, the fish market and the boats. Mutrah Souq, one of the oldest markets in the Arab world, hides a maze of covered alleys where you can smell frankincense from Dhofar and find Omani silver, khanjar daggers, pashminas and spices. On the hill above the bay stands Mutrah Fort, built by the Portuguese in the 16th century, a reminder of their control over this coast.
mct.al-alam: Al Alam Palace is the ceremonial palace of the Sultan of Oman, rebuilt in 1972 on the site of a much older royal residence. Its flamboyant façade, with blue and gold columns shaped like mushrooms, faces a large square and the harbour of Old Muscat. It is not open to visitors, but you can approach the gates for photos. The palace is flanked by the twin forts of Al Jalali and Al Mirani, built by the Portuguese in the 1580s on the rocks at either end of the cove, guarding what was once a strategic port on the route to India.
mct.national-museum-om: The National Museum of Oman, opened in 2016 opposite Al Alam Palace, tells the story of the country from prehistory to the present day across fourteen galleries. Highlights include the frankincense trade that made southern Arabia rich, the maritime history of Omani sailors who reached East Africa and China, traditional weapons, silver jewellery and the letter sent by the Prophet Muhammad to the rulers of Oman. Displays are in Arabic and English, and there is a learning centre for children. Allow at least an hour, as the collection is large.

fra.hauptwache: The Hauptwache is a small baroque building from 1730 that once housed the city guard and its prison. Today it gives its name to Frankfurt's busiest square and transport hub, where S-Bahn and U-Bahn lines meet below ground. From here the Zeil runs east: for decades one of Germany's busiest shopping streets, with department stores and the striking MyZeil mall, whose glass facade seems to be sucked into a vortex. Just around the corner stands St Catherine's Church, where the young Goethe was baptised.
fra.paulskirche: St Paul's Church is a round, red sandstone church finished in 1833. In 1848 and 1849 it hosted the Frankfurt National Assembly, the first freely elected parliament for all of Germany, which drafted a constitution with basic rights for citizens. The revolution failed, but its ideas and its black, red and gold colours lived on in today's German democracy. Burned out in 1944, the church was the first public building in Frankfurt to be rebuilt after the war and now hosts ceremonies such as the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade.
fra.roemer: The Römerberg is Frankfurt's historic heart. The Römer, the town hall with its stepped gables, has been the seat of the city government since 1405, and its Imperial Hall once hosted the coronation banquets of Holy Roman Emperors. Opposite stands a row of half-timbered houses, rebuilt in the 1980s after the old town was destroyed by bombing in 1944. In the middle is the Fountain of Justice, whose figure, unusually, wears no blindfold. In Advent the square fills with one of Germany's oldest Christmas markets.
fra.dom-fra: St Bartholomew's Cathedral is not technically a cathedral, as it never had a bishop, but for centuries it was the most important church in the Empire: German kings were elected here from 1356 and emperors were crowned here from 1562 to 1792. Its 95-metre Gothic tower can be climbed for a view over the river. Between the cathedral and the Römer lies the New Old Town, the DomRömer quarter, completed in 2018: fifteen faithful reconstructions and twenty new buildings along the old coronation route, recreating the medieval street pattern.
fra.eiserner-steg: The Eiserner Steg, the Iron Footbridge, was built in 1868 by citizens who were tired of paying for ferries and funded it themselves. Destroyed in the last days of the Second World War, it was rebuilt in 1946 and has become one of the city's landmarks. Couples attach love locks to its railings, and the inscription on the bridge quotes Homer's Odyssey in Greek. From the middle you get Frankfurt's classic postcard view: the cathedral on one side and the cluster of skyscrapers locals jokingly call Mainhattan on the other.
fra.museumsufer: The Museumsufer, the Museum Embankment, is a row of more than a dozen museums along the south bank of the Main, many housed in nineteenth-century villas. The most famous is the Städel, founded in 1815 by the banker Johann Friedrich Städel, with seven centuries of European art from Botticelli and Vermeer to Rembrandt, Monet and Picasso. Nearby are museums of film, architecture, applied arts and world cultures. On Saturdays a large flea market sets up along the river, and the wide grassy banks are perfect for a picnic.
fra.sachsenhausen: Alt-Sachsenhausen, on the south bank, is the traditional home of Frankfurt's Apfelwein, a dry, tart cider made from local apples. In the cobbled lanes around Klappergasse, taverns marked with a wreath of pine branches serve it in a ceramic jug called a Bembel and in ribbed glasses known as Gerippte. Guests share long wooden tables with strangers and order regional dishes such as Handkäs mit Musik, a tangy cheese with onions and vinegar, or Grüne Soße, the green sauce of seven herbs that Goethe is said to have loved.
fra.main-tower: At 200 metres, the Main Tower is the only skyscraper in Frankfurt with a public viewing platform. Completed in 1999, it is the headquarters of the Helaba bank and has a glass-walled restaurant near the top. A lift takes 45 seconds to reach the 54th floor, from where you see the whole financial district, including the European Central Bank's twin towers to the east, the river Main and, on a clear day, the Taunus hills. The terrace closes in storms and strong winds, and visitors pass an airport-style security check.

ber.reichstag: The Reichstag building was completed in 1894 to house the parliament of the German Empire. In 1933 it was set on fire, an event the Nazis used to suspend civil liberties, and in 1945 Soviet soldiers raised their flag on its roof. After reunification, the British architect Norman Foster rebuilt it with a glass dome, symbolising a transparent democracy, and since 1999 it has again been the seat of the Bundestag. A spiral ramp climbs inside the dome above the debating chamber; the visit is free but must be booked online in advance.
ber.brandenburger: The Brandenburg Gate was built between 1788 and 1791 on the model of the Propylaea in Athens and is crowned by the Quadriga, a chariot driven by the goddess of Victory. Napoleon carried the Quadriga off to Paris in 1806; it returned in 1814. During the Cold War the gate stood in the no-man's-land between East and West, a symbol of the divided city. On the night of 9 November 1989, crowds climbed the Wall in front of it, and since then it has been the symbol of German unity and the stage for the city's biggest celebrations.
ber.holocaust: The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, designed by the American architect Peter Eisenman and opened in 2005, covers almost two hectares near the Brandenburg Gate. It consists of 2,711 grey concrete slabs of different heights on an undulating floor. Walking between them, the ground sinks, the slabs rise above you and the city noise fades, creating a sense of isolation that each visitor interprets in their own way. Beneath the field, a free information centre tells the stories of individual victims and families.
ber.gendarmenmarkt: The Gendarmenmarkt is often called Berlin's most beautiful square. Laid out in the late seventeenth century, it is framed by two almost identical domed churches: the French Cathedral, built for the Huguenot refugees who settled in Berlin, and the German Cathedral. Between them stands the Konzerthaus, designed by Karl Friedrich Schinkel in 1821 as a theatre and now one of the city's great concert halls. The square takes its name from the Gens d'armes, a Prussian cavalry regiment whose stables once stood here.
ber.museumsinsel: Museum Island is the northern tip of an island in the river Spree where five world-class museums were built between 1830 and 1930. The Altes Museum, the Neues Museum with the bust of Nefertiti, the Alte Nationalgalerie, the Bode Museum and the Pergamon Museum together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Beside them rises the Berlin Cathedral, with its great green dome and the crypt of the Hohenzollern dynasty. In summer the lawns of the Lustgarten in front are a favourite place to rest.
ber.alexanderplatz: Alexanderplatz, named after the Russian Tsar Alexander I who visited Berlin in 1805, was rebuilt in the 1960s as the showcase square of East Berlin. Its landmarks are the World Time Clock, a popular meeting point, and the Television Tower: at 368 metres it is the tallest structure in Germany, built by the East German government in 1969. When the sun shines on its steel sphere, a cross of light appears, which Berliners nicknamed the Pope's revenge. A lift takes visitors to a viewing deck and a revolving restaurant.
ber.east-side: The East Side Gallery is a 1.3-kilometre stretch of the Berlin Wall along the river Spree, the longest surviving section. In 1990, shortly after the Wall opened, 118 artists from 21 countries painted murals on its eastern side. Among the most famous are Dmitri Vrubel's Fraternal Kiss, showing the Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev kissing the East German leader Erich Honecker, and Birgit Kinder's Trabant breaking through the Wall. At the end stands the red-brick Oberbaum Bridge, once a border crossing between the two halves of the city.

muc.marienplatz: Marienplatz has been the centre of Munich since the city's founding in 1158, and it takes its name from the golden Virgin Mary on a column erected in 1638. The square is dominated by the neo-Gothic New Town Hall, built between 1867 and 1908, whose tower holds the famous Glockenspiel. Every day at 11:00 and 12:00, and also at 17:00 from March to October, 32 life-size figures re-enact a royal wedding tournament of 1568 and the dance of the coopers, which celebrated the end of a plague. The tower also has a lift to a viewing gallery.
muc.viktualienmarkt: The Viktualienmarkt has been Munich's food market since 1807, when it moved here from the overcrowded Marienplatz. More than a hundred stalls sell fruit, vegetables, cheese, meat, fish, flowers and spices, and there are butchers serving warm Leberkäse in a bread roll. In the middle stands a tall maypole painted in the Bavarian blue and white, decorated with figures of the trades, and a beer garden where the six Munich breweries take turns serving their beer. Fountains honour famous local comedians and singers. The market is closed on Sundays.
muc.frauenkirche: The Frauenkirche, the Cathedral of Our Dear Lady, was built in just twenty years, from 1468 to 1488, using brick because there was no stone quarry nearby. Its twin towers, 99 metres high and topped with green onion-shaped domes added in 1525, are the emblem of Munich, and no building in the centre may be taller. Inside the entrance, look for the so-called Devil's Footprint in the floor: legend says the devil stamped here in rage after being tricked by the builder. The church was badly damaged in 1944 and rebuilt after the war.
muc.residenz: The Residenz was the palace of the Wittelsbach dukes, electors and kings who ruled Bavaria from 1508 to 1918. Over the centuries it grew into one of Europe's largest palace complexes, with ten courtyards and more than 130 rooms open to visitors, including the Antiquarium, a Renaissance hall full of ancient busts, and a treasury of crowns and jewels. In front lies Odeonsplatz, with the Feldherrnhalle, modelled on the Loggia dei Lanzi in Florence, and the yellow baroque Theatine Church. Beside them, the Hofgarten is a peaceful formal garden.
muc.englischer-garten: The English Garden, created in 1789, is one of the largest urban parks in the world, larger than New York's Central Park. It was designed in the informal English landscape style, with meadows, streams and woods. At its southern edge, by the Haus der Kunst, the Eisbach stream forms a standing wave where surfers ride all year round, even in winter. Further in are a Greek-style temple, the Monopteros, with a fine view of the city, and the Chinese Tower, surrounded by one of Munich's largest beer gardens.
muc.hofbraeuhaus: The Hofbräuhaus was founded in 1589 by Duke Wilhelm V as the royal court brewery, because he was unhappy with the expensive beer imported from northern Germany. The current beer hall dates from 1897. Under its painted vaulted ceilings, brass bands play while waiters carry litre steins called Maß to long wooden tables, some of which have been reserved for regular guests for generations, who keep their own stein in locked lockers. It is one of the most famous pubs in the world, popular with tourists and locals alike.
muc.olympiapark: The Olympic Park was built for the 1972 Summer Olympics, the first Games in Germany since 1936, designed to present a modern, cheerful and democratic country. Its tent-like roof of acrylic glass panels, by the architects Günter Behnisch and Frei Otto, spans the stadium, arena and swimming hall. The Games were overshadowed by the terrorist attack on the Israeli team, commemorated by a memorial in the park. Today you can climb the Olympic Hill or the Olympic Tower, and across the road visit BMW Welt, a free showroom, and the BMW Museum.

vie.stephansdom: St Stephen's Cathedral is the symbol of Vienna and the heart of the old town. The current Gothic building was largely built in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and its south tower, at 136 metres, was for a long time one of the tallest in Europe; locals affectionately call it the Steffl. The roof is covered with 230,000 glazed tiles forming a zigzag pattern and the double-headed eagle of the Habsburgs. Inside are the tombs of emperors and princes, and beneath it catacombs that hold the remains of thousands of Viennese.
vie.graben: The Graben, meaning moat, follows the line of the ditch of the Roman camp of Vindobona and is today one of Vienna's most elegant pedestrian streets. In the middle stands the baroque Plague Column, erected by Emperor Leopold I after the plague of 1679 killed tens of thousands. The Graben leads into the Kohlmarkt, lined with luxury shops, where Demel has made cakes and sweets since 1786, once as supplier to the imperial court. At its end, the dome of the Michaelertor announces the Hofburg palace.
vie.hofburg: The Hofburg was the winter residence of the Habsburgs for more than six hundred years, until the end of the monarchy in 1918, and today is the seat of the Austrian president. The sprawling complex of eighteen wings includes the Imperial Apartments of Franz Joseph and Elisabeth, the Sisi Museum devoted to the restless empress, the Imperial Treasury with the crown of the Holy Roman Empire, and the Spanish Riding School, where white Lipizzaner horses perform classical dressage. Michaelerplatz has Roman ruins visible in its centre.
vie.oper: The Vienna State Opera opened in 1869 with Mozart's Don Giovanni and was the first major building on the new Ringstrasse boulevard. Its directors have included Gustav Mahler and Herbert von Karajan, and with performances almost every evening from September to June it is one of the busiest opera houses in the world. Standing tickets go on sale on the day for just a few euros. Next door, the Albertina holds one of the largest collections of prints and drawings, from Dürer's Hare to Monet and Picasso, in a former Habsburg palace.
vie.naschmarkt: The Naschmarkt has been Vienna's most popular market since the sixteenth century, when milk bottles were traded here. Its name probably comes from naschen, to nibble. Today about 120 stalls stretch for more than half a kilometre along the Wienzeile, selling spices, olives, cheese, fruit, fish and specialities from Austria, the Balkans, Turkey and Asia, and there are many small restaurants. Along the street, Otto Wagner's art nouveau Majolica House shines with flower tiles. On Saturdays a flea market sets up at the end. Closed Sundays.
vie.karlskirche: St Charles's Church was promised by Emperor Charles VI during the plague of 1713 and dedicated to St Charles Borromeo, patron saint of plague victims. Designed by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach and completed in 1737, it combines a Greek temple portico, a great green dome and two columns modelled on Trajan's Column in Rome, carved with scenes from the saint's life. Inside, a panoramic lift takes visitors up to the frescoes of the dome. The pool in front reflects the whole facade, especially beautiful at dusk.
vie.schoenbrunn: Schönbrunn Palace was the summer residence of the Habsburgs. Its name comes from a beautiful spring found here by Emperor Matthias in 1612. Empress Maria Theresa turned it into a baroque palace with 1,441 rooms; the young Mozart played for her here at the age of six, and Franz Joseph was born and died here. The vast gardens, free to enter, climb to the Gloriette, a colonnade with views over the city. They also contain a palm house and the Tiergarten, founded in 1752 and the oldest zoo in the world still in operation.

prg.hrad: Prague Castle, founded around 880, is according to Guinness World Records the largest ancient castle complex in the world. For over a thousand years it has been the seat of Bohemian kings, Holy Roman Emperors and Czechoslovak and Czech presidents. At its centre rises St Vitus Cathedral, begun in 1344 and only completed in 1929, which holds the tomb of St Wenceslas and the Bohemian crown jewels. The circuit also includes the Old Royal Palace, the Romanesque St George's Basilica and Golden Lane, a row of tiny colourful houses where Franz Kafka once wrote.
prg.mala-strana: Malá Strana, the Lesser Town, was founded in 1257 on the slope beneath the castle. After a fire in 1541 the nobility built baroque palaces here, many of which now house embassies and the Czech parliament. Its centre is the Church of St Nicholas, a masterpiece of Prague baroque with a huge green dome and a frescoed ceiling; Mozart played its organ. The steep Nerudova street, leading up to the castle, still has its old house signs, such as the Two Suns and the Golden Horseshoe, used before houses had numbers.
prg.karluv-most: Charles Bridge was begun in 1357 under Emperor Charles IV, according to legend at 5:31 on 9 July, a palindromic date and time chosen for good luck. Built of sandstone blocks, it was for four centuries the only bridge across the Vltava. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries thirty baroque statues of saints were added; most are now copies. The most popular is St John of Nepomuk, thrown from the bridge in 1393: touching the bronze relief is said to bring you back to Prague. Gothic towers guard both ends.
prg.staromestske: Old Town Square has been Prague's marketplace since the twelfth century. Around it stand the twin spires of the Church of Our Lady before Týn, the baroque St Nicholas Church and the monument to the reformer Jan Hus, burned at the stake in 1415. On the Old Town Hall is the Astronomical Clock, installed in 1410 and the oldest still working: on the hour, the twelve apostles appear in the windows while a skeleton, Death, rings a bell. In front of the town hall, 27 crosses in the paving mark the execution of Bohemian leaders in 1621.
prg.josefov: Josefov, the Jewish Quarter, was home to one of the largest Jewish communities in Europe for centuries. Most of its old houses were demolished around 1900 to build elegant art nouveau streets, but six synagogues and the Old Jewish Cemetery survived. The Old-New Synagogue, from around 1270, is the oldest active synagogue in Europe and the setting of the legend of the Golem. The Pinkas Synagogue bears the names of nearly 80,000 Czech Jewish victims of the Holocaust, and in the cemetery about 12,000 gravestones are crowded together in layers.
prg.vaclavske: Wenceslas Square, really a boulevard 750 metres long, was founded by Charles IV in 1348 as a horse market. At its top stands the equestrian statue of St Wenceslas, patron of the Czech lands, in front of the National Museum. The square has witnessed the great moments of Czech history: the proclamation of Czechoslovakia in 1918, the self-immolation of the student Jan Palach in 1969 in protest against the Soviet occupation, and the huge demonstrations of the Velvet Revolution in November 1989, which ended communist rule peacefully.
prg.vysehrad: Vyšehrad, the High Castle, is a tenth-century fortress on a rock above the Vltava. According to legend, Princess Libuše stood here and foretold a great city whose glory would touch the stars, founding Prague. Today it is a quiet park inside baroque ramparts, with fine views over the river and the old town, far from the crowds. The neo-Gothic Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul has art nouveau paintings, and the cemetery next to it is the resting place of great Czech figures, including the composers Dvořák and Smetana and the painter Alfons Mucha.

sin.padang: The Padang, a large green playing field, has been at the heart of Singapore's civic life since the city was founded by Stamford Raffles in 1819. Around it stand the colonial monuments: St Andrew's Cathedral, the Victoria Theatre and Concert Hall, and the former Supreme Court and City Hall. On the steps of City Hall the Japanese surrender was signed in 1945, and Singapore's leaders were sworn in after independence. Since 2015 the two buildings have formed the National Gallery Singapore, the world's largest public collection of Southeast Asian art.
sin.merlion: The Merlion, with the head of a lion and the body of a fish, was created in 1964 as a logo for the tourism board. The lion recalls the city's name, Singapura, meaning lion city in Sanskrit, from the legend of a prince who saw a lion here in the fourteenth century; the fish tail represents its origins as a fishing village called Temasek. The 8.6-metre statue, erected in 1972, spouts water into Marina Bay. Facing it across the water are the Esplanade theatres, nicknamed the durians for their spiky shells, and Marina Bay Sands.
sin.mbs: The Helix Bridge, opened in 2010, is a pedestrian bridge whose steel structure is inspired by the double helix of DNA; at night it is lit with coloured lights. It leads to Marina Bay Sands, the resort designed by Moshe Safdie that has become the symbol of modern Singapore: three 55-storey hotel towers topped by a 340-metre-long SkyPark that looks like a ship. Its infinity pool is reserved for hotel guests, but the observation deck is open to all. Below are a shopping mall with a canal, the ArtScience Museum shaped like a lotus, and a casino.
sin.gardens: Gardens by the Bay opened in 2012 on reclaimed land as part of the vision of Singapore as a city in a garden. Its most famous sight is the Supertree Grove: eighteen tree-like structures up to 50 metres tall, covered with more than 160,000 plants, which collect rainwater and generate solar energy. A skywalk connects some of them, and every evening at 19:45 and 20:45 they light up to music in the free Garden Rhapsody show. The two cooled conservatories, the Flower Dome and the Cloud Forest with its 35-metre indoor waterfall, are paid.
sin.chinatown: Chinatown grew up in the nineteenth century when Raffles assigned this area to Chinese immigrants. Its narrow streets are lined with colourful two-storey shophouses, with businesses below and homes above. Surprisingly, the oldest Hindu temple in Singapore, the Sri Mariamman, built in 1827, stands on South Bridge Road, with its tower covered in gods. A few steps away, the Buddha Tooth Relic Temple, completed in 2007 in Tang dynasty style, houses a relic said to be a tooth of the Buddha and a peaceful rooftop garden. Both are free to visit.
sin.maxwell: Hawker centres are open-air food courts that the government built from the 1970s to move street vendors into hygienic, affordable premises. In 2020 Singapore's hawker culture was inscribed on UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. Maxwell Food Centre, opened in 1928, is one of the most famous, with more than a hundred stalls. The best known is Tian Tian, whose Hainanese chicken rice has been praised by international chefs. Locals reserve tables by leaving a packet of tissues, a habit called chope.
sin.little-india: Little India grew from the nineteenth century around Serangoon Road, where Indian workers looked after cattle and worked in brick kilns. Today it is the centre of Singapore's Tamil community, filled with the scent of jasmine garlands, spices and incense. The Sri Veeramakaliamman Temple, dedicated to the goddess Kali, dates from 1855. The Tekka Centre has a wet market, Indian food stalls and shops selling saris. The House of Tan Teng Niah, a colourful villa from 1900, is one of the most photographed buildings in the city. During Deepavali the streets are lit up.
sin.kampong-glam: Kampong Glam was the seat of the Malay royal family and the centre of the Muslim community after an 1819 treaty gave the area to the Sultan of Johor. Its landmark is the Sultan Mosque, rebuilt in 1932, with its golden dome; the base of the dome is decorated with the ends of glass bottles donated by poor Muslims so that everyone could contribute. Visitors are welcome outside prayer times, with robes provided. Nearby, Arab Street sells textiles, and Haji Lane is a narrow lane of murals, independent shops and cafés.

nyc.ny-911: You are standing where the Twin Towers rose until the morning of 11 September 2001. The two square pools sit exactly in their footprints, with water falling into a void that seems to have no bottom. Around the bronze edges are the names of the 2,977 people killed that day and the six who died in the 1993 bombing; on birthdays, staff place a white rose beside a name. Above you, One World Trade Center reaches 1,776 feet, a number chosen for the year of American independence. Look for the Survivor Tree, a pear tree pulled from the rubble and nursed back to life.
nyc.ny-wall: Wall Street takes its name from a real wall: a wooden palisade the Dutch built here in 1653 to protect New Amsterdam. Today it is the symbol of world finance. The temple-like building with the giant flag is the New York Stock Exchange, and across the street, on the steps of Federal Hall, a statue marks where George Washington took the oath as the first president in 1789. A few minutes south, the bronze Charging Bull appeared overnight in 1989, a guerrilla gift from artist Arturo Di Modica after a stock market crash.
nyc.ny-brooklyn: When it opened in 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was the longest suspension bridge in the world and the first to use steel wire. Its designer, John Roebling, died from an accident before work began; his son Washington took over until he was crippled by decompression sickness from the underwater caissons, and his wife Emily Roebling carried the engineering instructions to the site for over a decade. She was the first to cross. Walk up the wooden promenade to the first stone tower: behind you, the Financial District; ahead, the river and the Statue of Liberty in the distance.
nyc.ny-chinatown: Manhattan's Chinatown grew from a few streets in the 1870s, when Chinese workers moved east after building the railways, and it is now one of the largest Chinese communities outside Asia. Walk down Mott Street among fish markets, herbal shops and dim sum halls, and peek into Doyers Street, a crooked lane once called the Bloody Angle. Just north, Mulberry Street is what remains of Little Italy, where nearly ten thousand Italian immigrants once crowded into tenements; the San Gennaro festival still fills it every September.
nyc.ny-times: Times Square was called Longacre Square until 1904, when The New York Times moved into the tower at its southern tip. On New Year's Eve 1907 the newspaper dropped the first illuminated ball from its roof, a tradition watched today by a billion people. Around you are more than forty Broadway theatres, and the screens are so bright that the square is visible from aircraft. Sit on the red steps above the TKTS booth, where same-day theatre tickets are sold at a discount, and take in the crossroads of the world.
nyc.ny-rock: Rockefeller Center was built during the Great Depression, when John D. Rockefeller Jr. turned a failed opera-house project into fourteen Art Deco buildings that gave work to forty thousand people. Look for the golden Prometheus above the sunken plaza, the ice rink in winter, and the famous Christmas tree that has stood here since 1931. Across Fifth Avenue, St Patrick's Cathedral took twenty-one years to build and its spires were once the tallest point in the city; step inside for the rose window and a moment of calm.
nyc.ny-central: In the 1850s this land was swamp, rocky outcrops and shantytowns. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux won a competition to design a park for all classes, and workers moved more earth than for the Panama Canal locks. Walk down The Mall, a tunnel of American elms, to Bethesda Terrace, where the Angel of the Waters fountain looks over the lake and rowing boats. Every bridge in the park is different, and every bench plaque you see has been adopted by someone in memory of a person or a moment they loved here.
nyc.ny-highline: From 1934 freight trains ran along this elevated track, three storeys above the street, to deliver meat and milk straight into the warehouses of the Meatpacking District. The line was abandoned in 1980 and wild grasses took over. Two neighbours fought to save it from demolition, and in 2009 it reopened as a park planted to echo that wild landscape. Walk north among art installations and views down the avenues. Below the southern end, Chelsea Market occupies the old Nabisco factory where the Oreo cookie was invented in 1912.

was.dc-capitol: The white dome of the Capitol is the seat of Congress and the point from which the city's four quadrants are measured. George Washington laid the cornerstone in 1793; British troops burned the building in 1814, and the cast-iron dome you see was finished during the Civil War, when Lincoln insisted construction continue as a sign that the Union would survive. On top stands the Statue of Freedom. The Senate meets in the north wing and the House of Representatives in the south; a flag flies above each chamber when it is in session.
was.dc-library: The Library of Congress was founded in 1800 with a few hundred books; when the British burned it in 1814, Thomas Jefferson sold Congress his personal library of 6,487 volumes to start again. Today it holds more than 170 million items, the largest collection in the world, including a Gutenberg Bible. The Thomas Jefferson Building is a palace of marble, mosaics and murals; climb to the gallery above the Main Reading Room for one of the most beautiful interiors in America. Next door, the Supreme Court's motto reads Equal Justice Under Law.
was.dc-mall: The National Mall is America's front lawn, two miles of grass stretching from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial. Pierre L'Enfant drew it in 1791 as a grand avenue for the new capital. On both sides stand the Smithsonian museums, born from the bequest of James Smithson, a British scientist who never visited the United States but left his fortune to found an institution for the increase and diffusion of knowledge. All of them are free: dinosaurs and the Hope Diamond on one side, rockets and Van Gogh on the other.
was.dc-monument: At 555 feet, the Washington Monument was the tallest structure in the world when it was completed in 1884. Look closely about a third of the way up and you will see the marble change colour: construction stopped for more than twenty years because of a lack of money and the Civil War, and when it resumed the stone came from a different quarry. The fifty American flags around its base represent the states. By law, no building in central Washington may rise high enough to block the view of this obelisk.
was.dc-lincoln: The World War Two Memorial honours sixteen million Americans who served, with a gold star for every hundred who died. Beyond it, the Reflecting Pool leads to the Lincoln Memorial, a Greek temple with thirty-six columns, one for each state in the Union when Lincoln died. Inside, his statue sits nineteen feet tall, with the Gettysburg Address carved on the wall. On these steps, on 28 August 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his I Have a Dream speech to 250,000 people; an inscription marks the spot where he stood.
was.dc-whitehouse: Every president except George Washington has lived in this house. Construction began in 1792 and it was burned by British troops in 1814; it was rebuilt and painted white, and the name stuck. From Lafayette Square you see the north facade with its columned portico. The park is named after the Marquis de Lafayette, the young French aristocrat who fought for American independence. Across the square, St John's Church is known as the Church of the Presidents: since James Madison, every president has attended at least one service there.
was.dc-georgetown: Georgetown is older than Washington itself: it was a busy tobacco port on the Potomac by 1751, forty years before the capital was planned. Its Federal-style brick houses, cobbled streets and gas lamps survive almost intact. Walk along the C&O Canal, built to carry coal from the mountains, where mule-drawn boats once passed, and climb the steep Exorcist Steps, made famous by the 1973 horror film. On M Street and Wisconsin Avenue you'll find shops and cafés, and the waterfront park is perfect for watching rowers on the river at sunset.

sfo.sf-union: Union Square takes its name from the pro-Union rallies held here on the eve of the Civil War. The column in the middle, topped by a figure of Victory, celebrates Admiral Dewey's naval victory in 1898. Today it is the city's shopping heart. Walk a block south to the corner of Powell and Market and watch the cable cars arrive at the turntable, where the gripman and conductor push the car around by hand. San Francisco's cable cars are the last manually operated system in the world and a moving National Historic Landmark.
sfo.sf-chinatown: San Francisco's Chinatown is the oldest in North America, founded in the 1850s by immigrants who came during the Gold Rush and later built the railroads. It survived the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 and the earthquake and fire of 1906, after which it was rebuilt in the pagoda style you see today, partly to attract visitors. Enter through the Dragon Gate on Grant Avenue, look up at the temples above the shops on Waverly Place, and find the tiny alley where fortune cookies are still folded by hand.
sfo.sf-northbeach: North Beach was the landing place of Italian fishermen and, in the 1950s, the home of the Beat Generation. At City Lights Bookstore, Lawrence Ferlinghetti published Allen Ginsberg's poem Howl and was arrested for obscenity; he won the trial in a landmark case for free speech. Next door, Vesuvio Café was Jack Kerouac's bar. Washington Square, with the twin white spires of Saints Peter and Paul Church, is where locals practise tai chi in the morning, and where Joe DiMaggio posed for wedding photos after marrying Marilyn Monroe at City Hall.
sfo.sf-lombard: This block of Lombard Street was once too steep for cars, with a gradient of twenty-seven percent. In 1922 a property owner proposed eight hairpin bends to make it drivable, and it became known as the crookedest street in the world, though Vermont Street in the Potrero district is actually twistier. Walk down the steps on either side among hydrangeas and gardens. From the top you see Coit Tower, the bay and, on a clear day, the Bay Bridge. Cars descend at five miles an hour, and residents now pay to keep the crowds under control.
sfo.sf-wharf: Fisherman's Wharf grew from the moorings of Italian fishermen who sailed small boats called feluccas. Dungeness crab still comes in from October to June. At Pier 39, hundreds of California sea lions took over the boat docks after the 1989 earthquake and never left; they bark and sunbathe whatever the season. Look out to Alcatraz, the island prison that held Al Capone and closed in 1963. Try clam chowder in a sourdough bowl: the city's sourdough bread has been made with the same yeast cultures since the Gold Rush.
sfo.sf-ferry: Before the bridges were built in the 1930s, fifty thousand people a day crossed the bay by ferry and arrived at this building, opened in 1898. Its clock tower copies the Giralda of Seville. After the bridges were built, the ferries declined and a raised freeway blocked the view for decades, until the 1989 earthquake damaged it and the city chose to tear it down. Today the Ferry Building is a food hall of local producers: oysters, bread, cheese, coffee. On Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays a farmers market fills the square outside.
sfo.sf-goldengate: When it opened in 1937, the Golden Gate was the longest suspension bridge in the world, spanning the strait where the Pacific enters the bay. Its colour, International Orange, was meant to be a primer, but the architect Irving Morrow liked it because it blends with the hills and stands out in the fog. The towers rise 746 feet and the main cables contain enough wire to circle the Earth three times. Walk out on the east sidewalk to the first tower; below you, container ships and sailboats pass, and the wind can be strong and cold.

chi.chi-bean: Millennium Park sits on top of a railway yard and an underground car park, and it opened in 2004, four years late and far over budget, yet it quickly became Chicago's favourite place. Cloud Gate, nicknamed the Bean, is made of 168 stainless steel plates welded so smoothly that no seam is visible; it reflects the skyline and everyone underneath. Nearby, the two towers of the Crown Fountain display the faces of a thousand Chicagoans that spout water, and Frank Gehry's Pritzker Pavilion hosts free summer concerts under a trellis of steel.
chi.chi-art: Founded in 1879, the Art Institute is one of the world's great museums and a favourite of its visitors in surveys. The two bronze lions guarding the entrance wear wreaths at Christmas and team helmets when Chicago wins championships. Inside are icons of American art, including Grant Wood's American Gothic and Edward Hopper's Nighthawks, along with Georges Seurat's A Sunday on La Grande Jatte, one of the largest Impressionist collections outside Paris, and the Thorne miniature rooms, beloved by children.
chi.chi-river: In 1900 Chicago achieved something unique: it reversed the flow of its river so that sewage would no longer run into Lake Michigan, the city's drinking water. Today the river is the stage for its architecture. Walk along the Riverwalk past the Wrigley Building, the neo-Gothic Tribune Tower and Marina City's corn-cob towers. On Saint Patrick's Day the river is dyed bright green. Architecture boat tours leave from here and explain how, after the Great Fire of 1871, Chicago invented the skyscraper with steel frames.
chi.chi-mile: The Magnificent Mile is the stretch of Michigan Avenue north of the river, lined with department stores, hotels and boutiques. Its oldest survivor is the Water Tower, a small castle of yellow limestone built in 1869 to house a water pipe. Two years later, the Great Fire destroyed a third of the city and left a hundred thousand people homeless, but the tower survived and became a symbol of rebuilding. Look up at the John Hancock Center, now 875 North Michigan, whose X-braced structure is one of the city's engineering icons.
chi.chi-navy: Navy Pier stretches more than half a mile into Lake Michigan. Opened in 1916 as a cargo and passenger pier, it was used during the Second World War to train navy pilots, who practised take-offs and landings on aircraft carriers converted from lake steamers; dozens of wrecked aircraft still lie at the bottom of the lake. Today it has a Ferris wheel, gardens and boats. From the end of the pier you get the most famous view of the skyline. In summer, fireworks light up the lake on Wednesday and Saturday nights.
chi.chi-willis: Completed in 1973 as the Sears Tower, this was the tallest building in the world for twenty-five years. It is built from nine square tubes bundled together, a structural idea by engineer Fazlur Khan that allowed buildings to go higher with less steel. From the Skydeck on the 103rd floor, at 1,353 feet, you can see four states on a clear day: Illinois, Indiana, Michigan and Wisconsin. Step out into The Ledge, glass boxes that project from the facade, and look straight down at the streets below.

bos.bos-common: Boston Common was bought by the Puritan settlers in 1634 and used as cow pasture, militia training ground and place of public execution; British troops camped here before the Revolution. It is the oldest public park in the United States. Next to it, the Public Garden was the first public botanical garden in the country; its swan boats have carried passengers around the lagoon since 1877. Look for the bronze ducklings from the children's book Make Way for Ducklings. The red line in the pavement starts here: it's the Freedom Trail.
bos.bos-statehouse: The Massachusetts State House, completed in 1798, was designed by Charles Bulfinch on land that once belonged to John Hancock. Its dome was first covered in copper by Paul Revere's company and later gilded in 23-carat gold. During the Second World War it was painted grey to avoid being a target for bombers. Behind it climbs Beacon Hill, with brick sidewalks, gas lamps and Acorn Street, perhaps the most photographed street in America. In the chamber hangs the Sacred Cod, a carved wooden fish symbolising the fishing industry.
bos.bos-granary: The Granary Burying Ground, established in 1660, takes its name from a grain storehouse that stood next door. Here lie three signers of the Declaration of Independence: John Hancock, Samuel Adams and Robert Treat Paine, along with Paul Revere and the five victims of the Boston Massacre of 1770. Look at the slate headstones carved with winged skulls, a Puritan symbol of death. The graves are not where the stones are; they were rearranged in neat rows in the nineteenth century to make mowing the lawn easier.
bos.bos-faneuil: Faneuil Hall was given to the city in 1742 by the merchant Peter Faneuil, with a market below and a meeting hall above. In the 1760s and 1770s, Samuel Adams and other patriots gave speeches here against British taxes, and it earned the nickname Cradle of Liberty. The golden grasshopper on the weathervane has been there since 1742. Behind it, Quincy Market, built in 1826, is a long granite hall full of food stalls: this is the place to try a New England clam chowder or a lobster roll.
bos.bos-northend: The North End is Boston's oldest residential neighbourhood, settled in the 1630s, and since the late nineteenth century it has been the city's Little Italy. In Hanover Street you'll find cafés, pastry shops and endless debate over who makes the best cannoli. In North Square stands the Paul Revere House, built around 1680, the oldest building in downtown Boston. On the night of 18 April 1775, Revere left from here on his famous midnight ride to warn that British troops were marching on Lexington and Concord.
bos.bos-oldnorth: Christ Church, known as Old North, was built in 1723 and is Boston's oldest church still in use. On the night of 18 April 1775, sexton Robert Newman climbed the steeple and hung two lanterns, the agreed signal that the British were leaving Boston by sea across the Charles River rather than by land: one if by land, two if by sea. The poet Longfellow made the scene famous in 1860. Inside, the box pews are still owned by families, and the oldest bells in North America were rung here by a young Paul Revere.
bos.bos-harvard: Harvard, founded in 1636, is the oldest university in the United States. It took its name from John Harvard, a young minister who left his library and half of his estate to the college. In Harvard Yard, the bronze statue is known as the Statue of Three Lies: it says John Harvard, Founder, 1638, but he was not the founder, the college dates from 1636, and the face is not his, because no portrait existed. Touching his shoe is said to bring luck. Around the yard, Harvard Square has bookshops, cafés and street musicians.

mia.mia-lincoln: Lincoln Road was laid out in the 1910s by Carl Fisher, the developer who turned mangrove swamp into Miami Beach. In 1960 the architect Morris Lapidus closed it to cars and created one of America's first pedestrian malls, with sculptural shades, fountains and gardens. Today it is lined with cafés, galleries and shops. At its eastern end, the New World Center, designed by Frank Gehry, is the home of an orchestra academy; on some evenings concerts are projected onto a giant outdoor wall and the public watches for free from the park.
mia.mia-espanola: Española Way was built in 1925 as an artists' village in Mediterranean Revival style, inspired by the villages of Spain and the south of France. In the 1930s it became a lively nightspot, and legend has it that Desi Arnaz played the conga here before becoming famous in I Love Lucy. Today it is a pedestrian lane of pink facades, terracotta roofs, bougainvillea and restaurants. In the evening, string lights are switched on and the tables fill the street. It is a perfect place for a coffee or dinner away from the noise of Ocean Drive.
mia.mia-artdeco: South Beach has the largest concentration of Art Deco buildings in the world, more than eight hundred of them, built mainly between the 1920s and 1940s. In the 1970s, many were threatened with demolition, until a group led by Barbara Capitman created the Miami Beach Architectural Historic District in 1979, the first twentieth-century district on the National Register. At the Welcome Center you'll find maps and guided walks. Look for the classic details: porthole windows, eyebrow ledges for shade, neon signs and pastel colours.
mia.mia-ocean: Ocean Drive is the facade of Miami Beach: a row of Art Deco hotels in mint, pink and lemon, facing Lummus Park and the beach. By day, cyclists and skaters pass beneath the palm trees; at night, the neon signs light up the street. Look for the colourful lifeguard towers on the sand, each designed differently after Hurricane Andrew in 1992. At number 1116 stands the Villa Casa Casuarina, the Mediterranean mansion of fashion designer Gianni Versace, who was killed on its steps in 1997. Check prices before sitting down at a café here.
mia.mia-southpointe: South Pointe Park is the southern tip of Miami Beach, where Government Cut, the channel dug in 1905, connects Biscayne Bay to the Atlantic. Every evening the giant cruise ships of the Port of Miami, the busiest cruise port in the world, slide past just a few hundred feet away. Walk out on the 450-foot fishing pier for views of the beach and the downtown skyline. This was once an area of seedy bars; today it has gardens, dunes and a children's playground. It is one of the best places in the city to watch the sunset over the bay.
mia.mia-wynwood: Twenty years ago, Wynwood was a district of empty warehouses and garment factories. In 2009 the developer Tony Goldman invited street artists from around the world to paint the walls of six buildings, and the Wynwood Walls were born. Today it is one of the world's largest open-air street art museums, and murals cover almost every building in the area. The central enclosure has an entrance fee, but the surrounding streets are free to explore. Galleries, breweries and cafés have moved in, and the second Saturday of the month brings an art walk.

lax.la-olvera: Los Angeles began right here. In 1781 forty-four settlers from Mexico founded El Pueblo de la Reina de los Ángeles beside the river, and the Avila Adobe, built in 1818, is the oldest house still standing in the city. By the 1920s the plaza was run-down, until Christine Sterling turned Olvera Street into the colourful Mexican marketplace you see today, full of leather, candles and taquitos. Across Alameda Street, Union Station opened in 1939 and was the last of America's grand railway stations; step inside to see its Art Deco waiting room and tiled courtyards.
lax.la-gcm: Grand Central Market has fed downtown Los Angeles since 1917, when this was the city's smart shopping district. Generations of immigrants ran its stalls, and today old-timers selling chillies and dried beans sit beside queues for egg sandwiches, ramen and tacos. Opposite the entrance, Angels Flight, opened in 1901, is often called the shortest railway in the world: two little orange cars haul passengers up Bunker Hill in under a minute, as in the film La La Land. Across Broadway, the Bradbury Building of 1893 hides a glorious iron and glass atrium that starred in Blade Runner.
lax.la-disney: When the Walt Disney Concert Hall opened in 2003, Frank Gehry's curving stainless-steel sails changed the face of downtown. They were so reflective that the glare heated neighbouring flats, and some panels had to be sanded to a dull finish. The hall is home to the Los Angeles Philharmonic and its wooden auditorium is famed for its sound; climb the outside stairs to the hidden rooftop garden. Next door, The Broad holds the contemporary art collection of Eli and Edythe Broad, from Warhol to Basquiat. Entry is free with a timed reservation, and Yayoi Kusama's Infinity Mirror Room is the hardest slot to get.
lax.la-hollywood: Hollywood Boulevard is where the film industry put its fame in the pavement. The Walk of Fame began in 1960 and now counts more than 2,700 brass stars, including ones for fictional characters such as Mickey Mouse. The TCL Chinese Theatre, opened as Grauman's in 1927, keeps the handprints and footprints of stars in its forecourt; legend says the tradition began when an actress stepped into wet cement by accident. Look north to the hills for the Hollywood sign: it went up in 1923 reading Hollywoodland to advertise a housing estate, and lost its last four letters in 1949. Watch out for costumed characters who expect money for photos.
lax.la-griffith: Griffith Observatory has looked over Los Angeles since 1935. The land was given to the city by Griffith J. Griffith, a mining millionaire who wanted ordinary people to be able to look through a telescope, so by his wish entry is still free. Inside are a Tesla coil, a Foucault pendulum and one of the finest planetariums in the world. James Dean filmed Rebel Without a Cause on this terrace, and a bust of him faces the Hollywood sign. Come for sunset, when the grid of city lights spreads out to the ocean, and stay for the free public telescopes on clear evenings.
lax.la-santamonica: Santa Monica Pier opened in 1909 and its Ferris wheel, powered by solar panels, is the symbol of the Californian coast. A sign at the end of the pier marks the official finish of Route 66, the highway that once ran 2,400 miles from Chicago. Walk or cycle south along the beach path to Venice, founded in 1905 by Abbot Kinney, who dug canals to recreate the Italian city on the Pacific. Today Venice is famous for its boardwalk of street performers, the outdoor weights of Muscle Beach, the skate park and murals. Sunset over the water is the moment to be here.

las.lv-sign: The Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign has greeted drivers arriving from Los Angeles since 1959. It was designed by Betty Willis, a local commercial artist, who never copyrighted it because she considered it a gift to the city; that is why its image appears on everything from mugs to fridge magnets. The silver dollars behind the letters were a nod to Nevada, the Silver State. Strictly speaking the sign is not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise, like almost all of the Strip. A small car park sits in the central reservation, and there is usually a friendly queue for photos.
las.lv-bellagio: The Bellagio opened in 1998 as the most expensive hotel ever built, and its eight-acre lake is a nod to Lake Como in Italy. The fountains are its free show: more than 1,200 jets, some shooting water up to 460 feet into the air, dance to music by Sinatra, Pavarotti or Celine Dion every half hour in the afternoon and every 15 minutes in the evening. The finale of the film Ocean's Eleven was shot here. Inside, past the glass flowers of Dale Chihuly on the lobby ceiling, the Conservatory changes its garden of real flowers with every season.
las.lv-paris: Paris Las Vegas opened in 1999 with copies of the Arc de Triomphe, the Opéra and an Eiffel Tower built at half scale, about 540 feet high. The engineers used Gustave Eiffel's original drawings, but had to swap wrought iron for welded steel to meet fire codes. Three of the tower's legs plunge through the roof into the casino, and you can see them between the slot machines. A lift takes you to the viewing deck at the top, which looks straight down onto the Bellagio fountains across the street. At night the tower glitters and the hot-air balloon sign glows.
las.lv-caesars: Caesars Palace opened in 1966, built by Jay Sarno, who wanted every guest to feel like an emperor; he deliberately left the apostrophe out of the name. Statues, fountains and columns copy ancient Rome, and on New Year's Eve 1967 the daredevil Evel Knievel crashed spectacularly while jumping over the fountains on his motorbike. Inside, the Forum Shops of 1992 are covered by a painted sky that changes from dawn to dusk every hour, so shoppers lose track of time. The Colosseum theatre has hosted long residencies by Celine Dion and Elton John.
las.lv-venetian: The Venetian stands on the site of the Sands, the casino where Frank Sinatra and the Rat Pack performed in the 1960s. It opened in 1999 with replicas of St Mark's Campanile, the Doge's Palace and the Rialto Bridge, and indoor canals where gondoliers sing under a painted sky. Behind it rises the Sphere, opened in September 2023: a globe 366 feet tall whose skin is covered with about 1.2 million LED pucks. At night it turns into an eye, a basketball or the Earth itself, and you can watch it free from the street. Inside is a theatre with the largest high-resolution screen in the world.
las.lv-fremont: Fremont Street is the Las Vegas of the 1940s and 1950s, long before the Strip. The El Cortez, opened in 1941, is the oldest casino still in operation, and the neon cowboy Vegas Vic has waved from the Pioneer Club since 1951. As the Strip drew the crowds away, downtown fought back in 1995 by covering five blocks with a vaulted canopy, now carrying millions of LED lights and free light shows every hour after dark. The SlotZilla zip line flies people overhead. Nearby, the Neon Museum keeps the giant signs of demolished casinos, and the Mob Museum tells the story of the gangsters who built the city.

msy.nola-jackson: Jackson Square was laid out in 1721 as the Place d'Armes, the parade ground of French New Orleans. It was renamed after Andrew Jackson, who defeated the British here in 1815; his bronze statue on a rearing horse dates from 1856. Behind it stands St Louis Cathedral, the oldest cathedral in continuous use in the United States, rebuilt after the great fires of the 18th century and given its three spires in the 1850s. The red-brick Pontalba Buildings on either side, from the 1840s, are among the oldest apartment buildings in the country. Painters, tarot readers and brass bands fill the pavement all day.
msy.nola-cafe: Café du Monde has served the same thing since 1862: beignets, square doughnuts buried in powdered sugar, and café au lait made with chicory. Chicory was added to stretch coffee during shortages, including the Union blockade of the Civil War, and New Orleanians kept the taste. Sit under the green-and-white awning, order three beignets and try not to wear the sugar home. Next door, the French Market has operated since 1791 and is the oldest public market in the country; today it sells pralines, hot sauce, crafts and souvenirs. Climb the levee steps behind it to see the great curve of the Mississippi.
msy.nola-royal: Royal Street is the elegant side of the French Quarter, lined with art galleries, jewellers and antique dealers, some of them in business for over a century. Despite the name of the quarter, most of the buildings are Spanish: two great fires in 1788 and 1794 destroyed the French town, and it was rebuilt under Spanish rule with brick walls, courtyards and the lacy cast-iron balconies added later. In the afternoon several blocks close to cars and become a stage for street musicians, from jazz trios to tap dancers. Look for the cornstalk fence of a 19th-century mansion and the hidden courtyards behind carriage gates.
msy.nola-bourbon: Bourbon Street is named after the French royal House of Bourbon, not the whiskey. By night it becomes the city's loudest party, with neon, balcony bars and drinks in plastic go-cups, which are legal on the street here. For the soul of the city, step one block to St Peter Street and Preservation Hall, opened in 1961 to keep traditional New Orleans jazz alive when it seemed about to disappear. There is no bar and no air conditioning, just wooden benches, a worn room and some of the best musicians in town playing short sets every evening. Buy tickets ahead and arrive on time.
msy.nola-frenchmen: Frenchmen Street, in the Faubourg Marigny just downriver from the French Quarter, is where locals go to hear music. Within three blocks there are a dozen clubs, from the tiny Spotted Cat to the jazz room at Snug Harbor, and on a good night you can drift from brass band to blues to swing without paying much more than the price of a drink. Musicians expect you to tip the jar that goes round. At night, the Frenchmen Art Market fills a lot with lanterns and stalls of local artists. The Marigny was laid out in 1805 on the plantation of Bernard de Marigny, who is said to have introduced the dice game craps.
msy.nola-garden: The St Charles streetcar line has run since 1835, making it the oldest continuously operating street railway in the world. Its olive-green cars, built in the 1920s, are themselves listed historic monuments; open the windows and ride under the oaks of St Charles Avenue for a few dollars. Get off at Washington Avenue for the Garden District, where wealthy American newcomers built Greek Revival and Italianate mansions in the 19th century, in contrast to the Creole French Quarter. Look for the cornstalk-fence villa, Commander's Palace restaurant and the walled Lafayette Cemetery No. 1, where the dead are buried above ground; check whether it is open.

mco.orl-eola: Lake Eola is the heart of downtown Orlando. The fountain in the middle, built in 1957 and lit up in changing colours at night, has become the symbol of the city and appears on its flag. Swans glide across the water, including black swans and white mute swans, and you can hire a swan-shaped pedal boat to join them. A paved path of almost a mile circles the lake, past the Walt Disney Amphitheater where concerts are held. Every Sunday morning a farmers' market fills the eastern shore with growers, food trucks and live music, and the skyline reflects beautifully at sunset.
mco.orl-church: Orlando grew up around the railway. When the South Florida Railroad arrived in 1880, citrus growers and settlers followed, and the red-brick Church Street Station of 1889 still stands where the trains stopped. In the 1970s the street was revived as an entertainment district of saloons and music halls before Disney World eclipsed it; today its bars and restaurants are popular with locals after work. The SunRail commuter train still stops here. A few blocks south, the glass Dr. Phillips Center for the Performing Arts hosts Broadway tours, ballet and concerts.
mco.orl-winterpark: Winter Park was founded in the 1880s as a winter retreat for wealthy northerners, and it still feels like a small town. Park Avenue runs along a shady Central Park, lined with boutiques, cafés and wine bars, and the SunRail train stops right at the edge of the green. Rollins College, founded in 1885, sits at the southern end. The Morse Museum holds the largest collection of works by Louis Comfort Tiffany anywhere, including the jewel-like chapel he designed for the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, rescued after a fire at his Long Island estate. On Saturdays a farmers' market is held in the old railway depot.
