mco.orl-boat: Winter Park's Scenic Boat Tour has been running since 1938, making it one of Florida's oldest attractions. The pontoon boats glide across three lakes linked by narrow canals originally dug to float logs, so tight that the trees brush the sides of the boat. Your skipper points out mansions of old Florida families, the Mediterranean campus of Rollins College and birds such as herons, egrets and ospreys; with luck you may see an alligator sunning itself on the bank. The ride lasts about an hour and leaves on the hour from the dock at the end of Morse Boulevard.
mco.orl-idrive: International Drive is Orlando's avenue of attractions, eleven miles of hotels, restaurants and amusement parks between the city and the theme parks. It boomed after Walt Disney World opened in 1971 and Universal Studios followed in 1990. At ICON Park the Wheel, about 400 feet tall, turns slowly enough to admire the flat Florida landscape, its lakes and, on clear days, the distant towers of the theme parks. Around it you'll find a giant upside-down house, a wax museum, one of the world's tallest free-standing drop towers and an indoor skydiving tunnel. Come at sunset, when the wheel lights up.
mco.orl-disneysprings: Disney Springs is the one part of Walt Disney World you can visit without a ticket. It opened in 1975 as the Lake Buena Vista Shopping Village, became Downtown Disney and was reinvented in 2016 as a Florida waterfront town, with mock-historic springs, warehouses and a bridge. Entry and parking are free. You'll find the world's largest Disney store, restaurants by famous chefs, a Cirque du Soleil theatre and live bands. At The Boathouse you can ride in an amphicar, a 1960s car that drives straight into the lake and floats away. In the evening you may see fireworks from the nearby parks.

yyz.to-cn: When it was completed in 1976, the CN Tower was the tallest free-standing structure in the world at 553 metres, and it kept that title for more than thirty years. It was built by the Canadian National railway to broadcast television and radio signals over the new skyscrapers that were blocking them. Lifts with glass fronts climb to the main deck in under a minute. The glass floor, added in 1994, holds the weight of several hippos, and the brave can try the EdgeWalk, walking hands-free around the outside of the roof. Lightning strikes the tower around 75 times a year, safely, thanks to copper strips running to the ground.
yyz.to-stlawrence: Toronto's public market has stood on this spot since 1803. The South Market building incorporates the city's first proper city hall, from 1845, and the council chamber upstairs is now an art gallery. Downstairs, more than a hundred vendors sell cheese, fish, mustard and maple syrup, and in 2012 National Geographic named it one of the best food markets in the world. Do not leave without a peameal bacon sandwich: lean back bacon rolled in cornmeal, originally ground yellow peas, served on a soft roll. The market is closed on Sundays and Mondays, and on Saturdays the farmers' market opens at dawn.
yyz.to-distillery: In 1832 the millers James Worts and William Gooderham opened a windmill and soon a distillery by the lake; by the 1860s Gooderham & Worts was the largest distillery in the world, shipping whisky across the empire. When production ended in 1990 the site held the best-preserved collection of Victorian industrial buildings in North America, and many films have been shot in its cobbled lanes. Since 2003 the district has been car-free, with galleries, design shops, breweries, a chocolate maker and cafés inside the old brick warehouses. In November and December it hosts Toronto's Christmas market.
yyz.to-nathan: Toronto's City Hall, opened in 1965, was a daring choice: the Finnish architect Viljo Revell won an international competition with two curved towers of different heights embracing a low council chamber, which from the air looks like an eye. Revell died before it was finished. In front, Nathan Phillips Square, named after the mayor who championed the project, has a reflecting pool crossed by three arches that becomes a free skating rink in winter. The illuminated TORONTO sign was installed for the 2015 Pan American Games. Next door, Old City Hall of 1899 has faces of politicians carved as gargoyles by its annoyed architect.
yyz.to-kensington: Kensington Market began in the early 1900s as a crowded Jewish market where vendors sold from carts and front porches. Waves of Portuguese, Caribbean, Latin American and Asian immigrants followed, and each left shops behind, so today you can buy Jamaican patties, Chilean empanadas, Portuguese custard tarts and vintage clothes on a single block. The area was declared a National Historic Site in 2006 and resists chain stores. On the last Sunday of each month from May to October, Pedestrian Sundays close the streets to cars. Just east along Spadina Avenue lies one of North America's largest Chinatowns.
yyz.to-rom: The Royal Ontario Museum opened in 1914 and is Canada's largest museum of world culture and natural history. In 2007 the architect Daniel Libeskind added the Michael Lee-Chin Crystal, a jagged structure of glass and aluminium that bursts out of the old stone building onto Bloor Street; locals still argue about whether they love it. Inside are dinosaur skeletons, a bat cave, Egyptian mummies, a Chinese Ming tomb and important First Nations art. Around the corner, Yorkville was a hippie haven in the 1960s, where Joni Mitchell and Neil Young played in coffee houses; today it is the city's most luxurious shopping district.

mex.mx-zocalo: According to legend, the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan here in 1325 when they saw an eagle perched on a cactus devouring a snake, the image now on the Mexican flag. The Spanish built their capital on the ruins, and the Zócalo, officially the Plaza de la Constitución, is one of the largest squares in the world. The Metropolitan Cathedral took from 1573 to 1813 to complete, and because the city stands on the soft bed of a drained lake, it leans and sinks; look for the pendulum inside that measures the movement. The National Palace on the east side holds Diego Rivera's murals of Mexican history, free with ID.
mex.mx-templo: For centuries the great temple of the Aztecs lay buried under colonial streets. In 1978 electricity workers digging a trench uncovered a huge carved stone of Coyolxauhqui, the moon goddess, dismembered by her brother Huitzilopochtli, and the excavations that followed revealed the Templo Mayor. Dedicated to Huitzilopochtli, god of war and sun, and Tláloc, god of rain, it was rebuilt seven times, each version enclosing the last like layers of an onion. Walkways lead over the ruins and the museum displays offerings, masks and the eagle warriors. Closed on Mondays.
mex.mx-madero: Calle Madero was the main street of colonial Mexico City, and since 2010 it has been pedestrian, carrying tens of thousands of people a day between the Zócalo and the Alameda. Halfway along, the Casa de los Azulejos is an 18th-century palace covered in blue and white tiles from Puebla; since 1919 it has housed the Sanborns restaurant, where Zapata's revolutionaries were famously photographed having breakfast in 1914. At the western end rises the Torre Latinoamericana, completed in 1956 and one of the first skyscrapers built for an earthquake zone. It survived the strong earthquakes of 1957 and 1985, and its top floors have a viewing deck.
mex.mx-bellas: The Palacio de Bellas Artes was begun in 1904 by the Italian architect Adamo Boari in white Carrara marble, with an Art Nouveau exterior. The revolution stopped the works, and when it was finally completed in 1934 the interior was finished in Art Deco style. Its theatre curtain is a Tiffany glass mosaic of the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl, and the upper floors hold murals by Rivera, Orozco and Siqueiros, including Rivera's Man at the Crossroads, recreated after the Rockefellers destroyed the original in New York. Like much of the city, the heavy building has sunk several metres. In front lies the Alameda Central, the oldest public park in the Americas.
mex.mx-antropologia: The National Museum of Anthropology, opened in 1964 and designed by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, is one of the great museums of the world. In the central courtyard a single column supports an enormous concrete umbrella from which water falls like rain. The Mexica hall holds the Sun Stone, the 24-tonne carved disc found buried in the Zócalo in 1790, often wrongly called the Aztec calendar. Other halls hold giant Olmec heads, the reconstructed tomb of the Maya king Pakal and the cultures of every region. When the huge monolith of Tláloc, god of rain, was brought here in 1964, a storm broke over the city. Closed on Mondays.
mex.mx-condesa: Condesa and Roma are the leafy, Art Deco neighbourhoods where Mexico City goes to eat, drink coffee and walk the dog. Avenida Amsterdam, in Condesa, follows the oval of an old horse-racing track, and its central path is a lovely walk under the trees. Parque México, opened in 1927, is a showcase of Art Deco design, with a clock tower and a lake. Next door, Colonia Roma was built for the wealthy around 1900 with French-style mansions and gave its name to Alfonso Cuarón's Oscar-winning film. In March and April the jacarandas turn the streets purple.

rio.rio-selaron: In 1990 the Chilean artist Jorge Selarón began to cover the crumbling steps outside his house with fragments of tiles, in the green, yellow and blue of the Brazilian flag. Over more than twenty years he added over 2,000 tiles from more than 60 countries, many sent by visitors, plus hundreds of hand-painted images of a pregnant woman. He called it his tribute to the Brazilian people and said the work would only end on the day he died; he was found dead on the steps in 2013. The 215 steps link Lapa and Santa Teresa and appeared in music videos by Snoop Dogg and U2. Come early in the morning to avoid the crowds.
rio.rio-arcos: The Arcos da Lapa, completed in 1750, are the most striking monument of colonial Rio: 42 white arches, about 17 metres high, built as an aqueduct to bring water from the Carioca river to the fountains of the city centre. Since 1896 the arches have carried the tracks of the bonde, the yellow tram that climbs to the hill neighbourhood of Santa Teresa. Below them, Lapa was the bohemian quarter of Rio in the early 20th century and today is the heart of samba nightlife, with live music in old townhouses from Thursday to Saturday. At night, keep your belongings close in the crowds.
rio.rio-theatro: The Theatro Municipal opened in 1909, when Rio was the capital of Brazil and wanted to rival Paris; its façade and grand staircase were inspired by the Paris Opéra. The interior glitters with marble, onyx, gold leaf and stained glass. The square in front, Praça Floriano, is known as Cinelândia after the cinemas built around it in the 1920s, and has long been the stage for political rallies. Around it stand the National Library, the largest in Latin America, and the National Museum of Fine Arts. The Theatro offers one-hour guided tours from Tuesday to Saturday.
rio.rio-amanha: The Museum of Tomorrow opened in 2015 as the flagship of the redevelopment of Rio's old port for the 2016 Olympics. Designed by the Spanish architect Santiago Calatrava, its white structure stretches over the bay like the skeleton of a bird, and its exhibitions ask how we will live on the planet in the next fifty years. Along the Olympic Boulevard, the artist Kobra painted Etnias, a giant mural of five faces from five continents that set a world record. A short walk away lies the Valongo Wharf, a UNESCO World Heritage Site where hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans were landed; it is a place of memory worth visiting.
rio.rio-cristo: Christ the Redeemer was inaugurated in 1931 on the summit of Corcovado, 710 metres above the city. The statue is 30 metres tall on an 8-metre base, and its arms span 28 metres. It was designed by the Brazilian engineer Heitor da Silva Costa with the French sculptor Paul Landowski; the face was made by the Romanian Gheorghe Leonida. The concrete is covered with thousands of triangles of soapstone, applied by hand by local women. In 2007 it was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. The little rack railway, opened in 1884, climbs through the Tijuca forest in about twenty minutes; go early, before the clouds.
rio.rio-copa: Copacabana is four kilometres of sand between two forts, and one of the most famous beaches in the world. The promenade's black-and-white wave pattern was laid out by Roberto Burle Marx in 1970, inspired by the Rossio square in Lisbon. At the centre, the Copacabana Palace has welcomed film stars and royalty since 1923. Each lifeguard post, or posto, has its own crowd, and the kiosks sell coconut water and caipirinhas. On New Year's Eve about two million people dressed in white gather here for the fireworks and throw flowers into the sea for Iemanjá. Carry only what you need to the sand.
rio.rio-pao: Sugarloaf Mountain rises 396 metres straight out of Guanabara Bay. Its cable car, opened in 1912, was the first in Brazil and only the third in the world; the original wooden cars carried just 24 passengers. Today glass cabins climb in two stages, first to Morro da Urca and then to the summit, and James Bond fought the villain Jaws on the cable car roof in the film Moonraker. From the top you see the whole city: Copacabana, the forest, Niterói across the bay and Christ the Redeemer on his mountain. Sunset is the most beautiful moment, and the busiest, so buy tickets online.

bue.ba-mayo: The Plaza de Mayo is named after the May Revolution of 25 May 1810, the first step towards Argentine independence, and the small white pyramid in the middle was put up a year later. Since then every great moment in the country's history has happened here. On the east side is the Casa Rosada, the pink presidential palace, from whose balcony Eva Perón addressed the crowds. Since 1977 the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo have walked around the pyramid every Thursday to demand news of children who disappeared under the military dictatorship; their white headscarves are painted on the ground. The cathedral holds the tomb of General San Martín, and Pope Francis was archbishop here.
bue.ba-tortoni: Avenida de Mayo, opened in 1894, was the city's first great boulevard, inspired by Paris and Madrid, linking the Casa Rosada to the Congress. Its Belle Époque buildings hide theatres, old hotels and the Palacio Barolo of 1923, whose design follows Dante's Divine Comedy, from hell in the basement to paradise in the lighthouse. Café Tortoni, founded in 1858, is the oldest café in Argentina: writers such as Jorge Luis Borges and Alfonsina Storni and the tango singer Carlos Gardel sat at its marble tables. Order a cortado and chocolate con churros, and come back in the evening for a tango show in the basement.
bue.ba-obelisco: The Obelisco, 67.5 metres high, was built in just 31 days in 1936 to mark 400 years since the first founding of Buenos Aires. It stands on Avenida 9 de Julio, which porteños proudly call the widest avenue in the world, with up to 7 lanes in each direction. When Argentina wins a football championship, this is where the celebrations explode. Two blocks north stands the Teatro Colón, opened in 1908 after twenty years of building. Its horseshoe auditorium is regularly ranked among the three best opera houses in the world for acoustics, and the guided tour shows its marble foyer, its gilded hall and its huge workshops.
bue.ba-santelmo: San Telmo is the oldest neighbourhood in Buenos Aires. Wealthy families lived here until the yellow fever epidemic of 1871 drove them north, and their mansions were turned into conventillos, crowded tenements for the waves of European immigrants who arrived next, and where tango took shape. Today the cobbled streets are full of antique shops, bars and tango clubs. The covered San Telmo Market dates from 1897. On Sundays the Feria de San Pedro Telmo fills Defensa Street with stalls, and couples dance tango in Plaza Dorrego. At the corner of Chile and Defensa, sit beside the bronze statue of Mafalda, Quino's beloved comic strip girl.
bue.ba-boca: La Boca grew up at the mouth of the Riachuelo, where Italian immigrants, mostly from Genoa, worked in the port and built houses of wood and corrugated iron. They painted them with paint left over from the ships, which is why each wall is a different colour. In the 1950s the painter Benito Quinquela Martín turned the old railway alley of Caminito, named after a 1926 tango, into an open-air museum. A few blocks away stands La Bombonera, the stadium of Boca Juniors, where Diego Maradona played; on match days the whole neighbourhood shakes. Stay in the tourist area and leave before dark.
bue.ba-recoleta: Recoleta Cemetery was founded in 1822 in the garden of a Recollect friars' monastery and is the most famous resting place in Argentina. It is a true city of the dead, with streets and squares lined by more than 4,600 marble vaults in every style, from Greek temples to Art Nouveau chapels, and over 90 of them are national monuments. Presidents, generals and writers lie here, and the most visited tomb is that of the Duarte family, where Eva Perón is buried. Look for the statue of Rufina Cambaceres, said to have been buried alive. Around the cemetery are cafés, the Recoleta cultural centre and the giant steel flower of Floralis Genérica, which opens and closes.

rak.rak-koutoubia: The Koutoubia minaret, 77 metres tall, has guided travellers into Marrakech since the 12th century. It was built under the Almohad caliphs, and its proportions inspired two famous sisters: the Giralda in Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat. The name comes from the kutubiyyin, the booksellers whose stalls once crowded its foot. The first mosque on the site was found to be misaligned with Mecca and was rebuilt alongside; you can still see the foundations of the original next to the garden. Local rules say no building in the medina may rise above the height of a palm tree, so the minaret still rules the skyline, and five times a day its call to prayer sets the rhythm of the city.
rak.rak-jemaa: Jemaa el-Fna has been the stage of Marrakech for a thousand years. In the morning there are orange-juice stalls, henna painters and water sellers in red costumes; by afternoon, storytellers, Gnawa musicians with iron castanets and acrobats; and at dusk, dozens of smoking food stalls turn the square into an open-air restaurant. In 2001 it was one of the first places in the world recognised by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, after a campaign by the writer Juan Goytisolo. Performers expect a coin if you photograph them, and it is kinder not to pay for photos with chained monkeys.
rak.rak-souks: North of the square begins the maze of souks, each lane once devoted to a single trade: leather, copper, carpets, lanterns and the dyers' souk, where skeins of wool hang to dry in every colour. Haggle with a smile and don't be afraid to walk away. At the end of the maze stands the Ben Youssef Madrasa, rebuilt in 1565 by the Saadian sultans, once the largest Koranic school in North Africa, where up to 900 students lived in tiny cells around a courtyard of carved cedar, stucco and zellige tiles. It reopened after restoration in 2022. Nearby, Le Jardin Secret is a peaceful restored riad garden.
rak.rak-bahia: Bahia means brilliance, and the palace was meant to be the most beautiful of its time. It was built at the end of the 19th century by the grand vizier Si Moussa and his son Ba Ahmed, who ruled Morocco in all but name while the young sultan was a child. Craftsmen from Fès spent years on its painted cedar ceilings, carved plaster and zellige mosaics, and the courtyards, apartments and gardens cover eight hectares. Rooms were arranged around the vizier's four wives and many concubines. Look for the great marble courtyard and the garden of orange trees, banana plants and jasmine.
rak.rak-saadian: The Saadian Tombs hold the sultans of the Saadian dynasty, who ruled Morocco in the 16th century. The greatest of them, Ahmad al-Mansur, filled the royal mausoleum with Italian Carrara marble, gilded cedar and stucco, traded for its weight in sugar. A century later the sultan Moulay Ismail, wanting to erase his predecessors, walled the tombs off, and they were forgotten until a French survey rediscovered them in 1917. The Hall of the Twelve Columns is the masterpiece, and there is often a short queue to look in. Nearby, the carved stone gate of Bab Agnaou is one of the oldest entrances to the Kasbah.
rak.rak-majorelle: The French painter Jacques Majorelle began creating this garden in 1923, collecting cacti, bamboo and palms from five continents and painting the walls of his studio an electric blue that now bears his name. When it was threatened by a hotel project in 1980, the fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent and his partner Pierre Bergé bought it and restored it, and Saint Laurent's ashes were scattered here. The studio now houses a museum of Berber culture, and next door the Yves Saint Laurent Museum, opened in 2017, shows his designs inspired by Morocco. Tickets are sold online for timed slots.

cas.cas-unite: Casablanca grew in a few decades from a small port into Morocco's biggest city, and the French planner Henri Prost laid out this square in the 1920s as its administrative heart. Around it stand the courthouse, the post office, the Bank Al-Maghrib and the clock tower of the Wilaya, all in the neo-Moorish style the French called Mauresque, with arches, green tiles and carved wood. Along Boulevard Mohammed V runs one of the richest collections of Art Deco buildings in the world, with wrought-iron balconies and stucco sunbursts. The local association Casamémoire organises walks to save and explain them.
cas.cas-sacrecoeur: The Sacré-Cœur Cathedral was built in 1930 by the architect Paul Tournon, a white concrete mix of Gothic lines, Art Deco detail and Moorish touches, with two slender towers that once dominated the city. After Moroccan independence in 1956 it stopped being used for worship, and today it is a cultural centre that hosts exhibitions and concerts. Beside it, the Parc de la Ligue Arabe, laid out in 1918, is the city's great green lung, with rows of palm trees, fountains and cafés, recently renovated. Walk through it in the late afternoon, when families come out for the cool air.
cas.cas-habous: The Habous quarter was built by the French from 1916 as a new medina for Moroccans moving to the booming city from the countryside. Architects reinterpreted traditional design, so the streets are orderly and shaded by arcades, with fountains, small squares and whitewashed walls. Next to the royal palace of Casablanca, it is known for its booksellers, olive and spice merchants and craft shops. The Mahkama du Pacha, the old courthouse, has dozens of rooms decorated with carved stucco and cedar. Do not leave without a box of almond pastries from Pâtisserie Bennis, in business since the 1930s.
cas.cas-medina: The old medina is small compared with those of Fès or Marrakech, and most of what you see dates from the 18th and 19th centuries, after the earthquake of 1755 and the city's refounding by Sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah. Its walls enclose narrow lanes of tailors, cheap electronics and household goods, and locals rather than tourists do their shopping here. On the seaward side, the Skala bastion still points old cannons towards the Atlantic, and its terrace restaurant is lovely at sunset. The Portuguese once called the town Casa Branca, the white house, which became Dar el Beida in Arabic and Casablanca in Spanish.
cas.cas-hassan: The Hassan II Mosque, completed in 1993, was built partly over the Atlantic, inspired by the Koranic verse that God's throne was upon the water. Its minaret rises 210 metres, one of the tallest in the world, and at night a laser beam at the top points towards Mecca. Around ten thousand craftsmen worked on the marble, carved cedar, stucco and zellige; the prayer hall holds 25,000 worshippers and the esplanade 80,000 more, and the roof can slide open to the sky. It is one of the few mosques in Morocco open to non-Muslims, on guided tours outside prayer times; dress modestly.
cas.cas-corniche: The Corniche of Ain Diab is where Casablanca comes to breathe: a long promenade of beaches, beach clubs, cafés and surf schools on the Atlantic. Joggers and families fill it at sunset, and on summer nights it stays busy until late. At its western end, on a rock just offshore, stands the white shrine of Sidi Abderrahmane, a 19th-century Sufi saint; at low tide people wade across, though non-Muslims may not enter the shrine itself. The El Hank lighthouse, built in 1916, guards the coast between the Corniche and the city.

cpt.cpt-company: In 1652 the Dutch East India Company sent Jan van Riebeeck to the Cape to grow vegetables for ships sailing to Asia, and this garden is the result: the oldest garden in South Africa. Today it is a shady park crossed by an avenue of oaks, with the Houses of Parliament, the Iziko South African Museum and the National Gallery around it. The squirrels were introduced by Cecil Rhodes. At its lower end stands St George's Cathedral, where Archbishop Desmond Tutu preached against apartheid, and the Slave Lodge, which tells the story of the thousands of enslaved people who built the early colony.
cpt.cpt-bokaap: Bo-Kaap, on the slopes of Signal Hill, is the historic home of the Cape Malay community, descendants of enslaved people and political exiles brought by the Dutch from Indonesia, India and East Africa. The Auwal Mosque, founded in 1794, was the first mosque in South Africa, and Afrikaans was first written down here in Arabic script. The houses are painted in bright pinks, greens and blues; one story says residents began painting them after they were finally allowed to own their homes. The Bo-Kaap Museum occupies a house from the 1760s. Remember that these are family homes, not a stage set.
cpt.cpt-castle: The Castle of Good Hope, built between 1666 and 1679, is the oldest surviving colonial building in South Africa. Its five bastions form a pentagon, and it once stood on the shoreline before land was reclaimed from the sea. Inside are military exhibits and the William Fehr collection of paintings and furniture. A short walk away, the District Six Museum tells the story of a lively mixed neighbourhood declared a whites-only area in 1966 under apartheid laws; about 60,000 people were forcibly removed and their homes bulldozed. Former residents often guide visitors, and the floor map is covered with their handwritten memories.
cpt.cpt-waterfront: The V&A Waterfront is named after Queen Victoria and her son Prince Alfred, who tipped the first load of rock for the harbour breakwater in 1860. The working harbour now mixes fishing boats with shops, restaurants and the Watershed craft market, and Cape fur seals often lounge on the quays. In Nobel Square stand statues of South Africa's four Nobel Peace Prize winners: Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, F. W. de Klerk and Nelson Mandela. The Zeitz MOCAA museum fills a 1920s grain silo with contemporary African art, and ferries leave from the Nelson Mandela Gateway for Robben Island, where Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in prison.
cpt.cpt-tablemtn: Table Mountain rises about 1,085 metres above the city, its flat top three kilometres long. When the south-easterly wind blows, a white cloud spills over the edge, known as the tablecloth. The cableway has run since 1929, and since 1997 its cars rotate as they climb, so everyone gets the view. The mountain lies in the Cape Floral Kingdom, the smallest and richest of the world's plant kingdoms, with more plant species on its slopes than in the whole of the British Isles; look for proteas and dassies, small furry rock hyraxes. In 2011 it was named one of the New Seven Wonders of Nature. Always check whether the cableway is open: it closes in high wind.
cpt.cpt-kirstenbosch: Kirstenbosch, founded in 1913 on land left to the nation by Cecil Rhodes, was the first botanical garden in the world devoted to a country's native flora. It stretches up the eastern slopes of Table Mountain, with proteas, ericas, cycads and a fragrance garden. The Boomslang, a curving steel walkway named after a tree snake, winds through the forest canopy and was built for the garden's centenary. A hedge of wild almond planted by Jan van Riebeeck in 1660 to mark the colony's boundary still survives. In summer, Sunday sunset concerts on the lawns are a Cape Town tradition.

zan.znz-forodhani: Forodhani Gardens were laid out in 1936 for the silver jubilee of Sultan Khalifa and restored in 2009 by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture. By day it is a shady seafront park where boys dive from the sea wall into the harbour. As the sun sets, dozens of stalls light their grills and the night market begins: skewers of lobster, octopus and kingfish, sugar-cane juice pressed with ginger and lime, and Zanzibar pizza, a thin dough stuffed with egg and meat or banana and chocolate and fried on a griddle. Agree on the price before the food goes on the grill.
zan.znz-fort: The Old Fort, Ngome Kongwe in Swahili, was built by Omani Arabs around 1700 after they drove the Portuguese out of Zanzibar, on the site of a Portuguese church. Its brown walls and crenellated towers are the oldest building in Stone Town. Over the centuries it served as a garrison, a prison and a railway depot; today its courtyard holds craft shops, a café and an open-air amphitheatre. It is one of the main venues of the Zanzibar International Film Festival and of Sauti za Busara, the great African music festival held every February.
zan.znz-palace: The House of Wonders, Beit al-Ajaib, was built in 1883 by Sultan Barghash as a ceremonial palace, and it was the first building in East Africa to have electricity and a lift, which gave it its name. It was damaged in 1896 during the Anglo-Zanzibar War, which lasted under an hour and is known as the shortest war in history. Part of the building collapsed in 2020 during restoration, and it is still being rebuilt. Next door, the Palace Museum, a 19th-century residence of the sultans, shows their furniture and a room dedicated to Princess Salme, who eloped with a German merchant and wrote the first known autobiography by an Arab woman.
zan.znz-cathedral: Christ Church Cathedral stands on the site of the last open slave market in East Africa, closed in 1873 under British pressure. Building began that same year, and the altar is said to stand where the whipping post once was. Inside, a crucifix is made from the wood of the tree under which David Livingstone's heart was buried. Beneath a nearby building you can enter two cramped underground chambers where captives were held before sale. In the garden, a sculpture of chained figures stands in a pit, a powerful memorial to the many thousands of people sold here. The visit includes a guide and a small museum.
zan.znz-darajani: Darajani is the market where all of Zanzibar does its shopping. Under the old covered halls and in the lanes around them you find fish and octopus brought in at dawn, bananas, mangoes and jackfruit, and heaps of spices. In the 19th century Zanzibar produced most of the world's cloves, and the island is still called the Spice Island; look for cloves, cinnamon, cardamom, nutmeg and vanilla. Kanga and kitenge cloths hang in bright rows, each kanga printed with a Swahili proverb. It is busy, noisy and fascinating; keep your bag close and ask before photographing people.
zan.znz-prison: Changuu, better known as Prison Island, lies thirty minutes by boat from Stone Town. In 1893 the British built a prison here for rebellious slaves, but it never held any prisoners and was later used as a quarantine station for yellow fever. Today the island is famous for its giant Aldabra tortoises, descendants of four sent as a gift from the Seychelles in 1919; some are well over a hundred years old, and you can feed them leaves. Around the island the water is clear, with coral and fish for snorkelling. Boats leave from the beach near Forodhani; agree the price and the time back.

tun.tun-bourguiba: Avenue Habib Bourguiba, named after the first president of independent Tunisia, was laid out by the French as the main boulevard of their new town, between the medina and the lake. Under its ficus trees stand the Cathedral of St Vincent de Paul of 1897, with its mix of Romanesque and Byzantine styles, and the Municipal Theatre of 1902, an Art Nouveau jewel. On 14 January 2011 tens of thousands of Tunisians gathered here in front of the Interior Ministry, shouting «Dégage!», until President Ben Ali fled; it was the start of the Arab Spring. Today it is the city's favourite place for coffee and an evening stroll.
tun.tun-babbhar: Bab el Bhar, the Sea Gate, also called the Porte de France, marked the boundary between the medina and the European town the French built on land reclaimed from the lake. Pass through it and you step from the 19th century into a city founded more than thirteen centuries ago. The medina of Tunis, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979, holds around 700 monuments, palaces, mosques, madrasas and fountains, in a maze of lanes that has changed little. Two main streets lead from the gate to the Zitouna Mosque, lined with souvenir stalls at first and then with the old trades.
tun.tun-zitouna: The Zitouna Mosque, the Mosque of the Olive Tree, is the heart of the medina and one of the oldest in North Africa. It was founded in the early 8th century and rebuilt in 864 by the Aghlabid rulers, reusing nearly two hundred columns from the ruins of Carthage. Its university, Ez-Zitouna, is one of the oldest centres of learning in the world. All around, the souks are still arranged by trade: Souk el Attarine sells perfumes and essences, Souk ech-Chaouachia makes the red felt chechia caps, and the goldsmiths fill the Souk el Berka. Non-Muslims may view the courtyard from the entrance at limited times.
tun.tun-dar: Dar Ben Abdallah is an 18th-century palace hidden behind a plain door in the southern medina. Its courtyard of marble columns, tiles and carved plaster now houses a museum of traditional life in Tunis, with costumes, jewellery and rooms set out as they were for weddings and daily life. A few lanes away, Tourbet el Bey is the mausoleum of the Husseinite beys who ruled Tunisia from the 18th century, a series of domed rooms covered in Italian marble, tiles and stucco, with the tombs topped by stone turbans and fezzes. These quiet streets show the medina behind the souks.
tun.tun-bardo: The Bardo Museum, opened in 1888 in a 19th-century palace of the beys, holds the largest collection of Roman mosaics in the world. The floors of villas from across Tunisia, once the Roman province of Africa, show sea gods, hunting scenes, harvests and circus races in brilliant colour. Its most famous piece is the only known portrait of the poet Virgil, seated between two Muses. The museum also covers Punic, Christian and Islamic history. A memorial at the entrance remembers the victims of the 2015 attack; the museum reopened in 2023 after a long closure. It is closed on Mondays.
tun.tun-sidibou: Sidi Bou Said, on a cliff above the Gulf of Tunis, takes its name from a 13th-century Sufi saint. Since 1915, at the urging of Baron Rodolphe d'Erlanger, whose palace is now a museum of Arab music, the village has been all white walls and blue doors, windows and studded gates. Paul Klee came here in 1914 and said colour had taken hold of him. Sit in the Café des Nattes with a pine-nut tea and watch the bay. On the way, stop at Carthage, founded according to legend by Queen Dido in 814 BC and destroyed by Rome in 146 BC, where the seaside Antonine Baths are the largest Roman baths in Africa.

add.add-unity: Unity Park opened in 2019 inside the grounds of the palace built by Emperor Menelik II, who founded Addis Ababa with Empress Taytu in 1886; the name means new flower. For over a century the compound was closed to the public. Now you can walk through Menelik's banquet hall and church, the throne room and offices of Emperor Haile Selassie, the parliament buildings and gardens representing every region of Ethiopia. There is also a small zoo with black-maned Ethiopian lions, once a symbol of the emperors. Tickets have a higher price for foreigners, and it is closed on Mondays.
add.add-trinity: Holy Trinity Cathedral, Kidist Selassie, was built in the 1940s to celebrate Ethiopia's liberation from Italian occupation and is the most important Orthodox church in the city. Its stained-glass windows and murals are by the painter Afewerk Tekle. Emperor Haile Selassie and Empress Menen were reburied here in 2000 in granite tombs beside the altar. In the churchyard lie patriots who fought the occupation and the British campaigner Sylvia Pankhurst, a lifelong friend of Ethiopia. Take off your shoes if asked, and women should cover their hair inside.
add.add-museum: The National Museum of Ethiopia is home to Lucy, known in Ethiopia as Dinkinesh, meaning you are marvellous. She is a 3.2-million-year-old skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis found in 1974 at Hadar in the Afar region, and named after the Beatles song «Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds» that was playing in the scientists' camp that night. The basement also displays Selam, a child of the same species about 3.3 million years old. Upstairs, galleries show Aksumite crowns, imperial furniture including Haile Selassie's throne, and modern Ethiopian painting. Ethiopia is often called the cradle of humankind, and this is the place to see why.
add.add-piazza: Piazza, or Arada, is the old commercial heart of Addis Ababa, rebuilt during the Italian occupation of 1936–1941 with arcades, cinemas and cafés. Here stands the Taitu Hotel, opened in 1898 as the country's first hotel, and the Tomoca coffee house, roasting beans since 1953. Ethiopia is where coffee was born: legend says a goatherd named Kaldi noticed his goats dancing after eating the red berries of a shrub in the Kaffa region. Order a macchiato standing at Tomoca's counter, or a traditional buna, and buy freshly roasted beans to take home.
add.add-merkato: Merkato is often described as the largest open-air market in Africa, covering several square kilometres of lanes and sheds west of the centre. It was established by the Italians in the 1930s and today sells almost everything: spices and coffee, baskets and furniture, livestock, electronics and gold. The most fascinating corner is Minalesh Tera, the recyclers' quarter, where old tyres become sandals and tin cans become stoves. It is crowded and chaotic, and pickpockets work the busiest lanes. Leave valuables at the hotel and, if you can, go with a local guide who knows the way through.
add.add-entoto: Before Addis Ababa existed, Emperor Menelik II had his capital on Mount Entoto, at around 3,000 metres. He was crowned in the church of Entoto Maryam in 1882, before moving down to the warm springs in the valley where the new city grew. The slopes are covered with eucalyptus trees, imported from Australia in Menelik's time for firewood, and women still carry bundles of branches down to the markets. Entoto Park, opened in 2020, has walking trails, viewpoints over the city and cafés. Long-distance runners train on these hills at dawn, breathing the thin air that makes champions.

nbo.nbo-museum: Nairobi began in 1899 as a depot on the railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria, on a swamp the Maasai called Enkare Nyrobi, the place of cool waters. The National Museum, founded in 1910 by naturalists and housed here since 1930, tells the story of Kenya's land, wildlife and peoples. Its human origins gallery shows fossils from Lake Turkana, including Turkana Boy, a nearly complete skeleton of a youth who lived about 1.6 million years ago. There are halls of birds and mammals, paintings by Joy Adamson of Kenya's peoples, and gardens with a snake park next door.
nbo.nbo-kicc: The Kenyatta International Convention Centre, completed in 1973, was designed by the Norwegian architect Karl Henrik Nøstvik with the Kenyan David Mutiso. Its 28-storey tower ends in a round crown, and beside it the low amphitheatre is shaped like a traditional African hut. For years it was the tallest building in Nairobi. Today you can climb to the rooftop helipad for one of the best views of the city: the skyline, the parliament, Uhuru Park and, on rare clear days, the snowy peak of Kilimanjaro far to the south. In front stands the statue of Jomo Kenyatta, Kenya's first president.
nbo.nbo-sheldrick: The Sheldrick Wildlife Trust was founded in 1977 by Daphne Sheldrick in memory of her husband David, a warden of Tsavo National Park. She was the first person to successfully hand-rear milk-dependent orphaned elephants, after years of experiments with formulas, and the trust has since raised hundreds of orphans and returned them to the wild. Every day from 11 to noon, the youngest elephants come out to drink giant bottles of milk and play in a mud bath while keepers explain each orphan's story. Visits must be booked online, and you can adopt an elephant and follow its progress.
nbo.nbo-giraffe: The Giraffe Centre was founded in 1979 by Jock and Betty Leslie-Melville to save the Rothschild's giraffe, of which only about 130 then remained in Kenya. Their breeding programme has helped reintroduce giraffes to several national parks. From a raised wooden platform you can look these gentle giants in the eye and feed them pellets; they take them with a long, rough purple tongue. Next door, the Giraffe Manor hotel is famous for giraffes poking their heads through the breakfast-room windows. A nature trail behind the centre leads through a small forest sanctuary.
nbo.nbo-karen: From 1917 to 1931 the Danish writer Karen Blixen ran a coffee farm here at the foot of the Ngong Hills, and she described those years in «Out of Africa», published in 1937 under the pen name Isak Dinesen. The 1985 film with Meryl Streep and Robert Redford made the story famous worldwide. The farmhouse, with its veranda and old furniture, was given to Kenya by the Danish government in 1964 and is now a museum. In the garden you can still see old farm machinery. The surrounding suburb, Karen, carries her name.
nbo.nbo-bomas: Bomas of Kenya, opened in 1971, is an open-air museum of the country's many ethnic groups; a boma is a traditional homestead. Walking through the grounds you can enter reconstructed homesteads of peoples such as the Kikuyu, Luo, Maasai, Kalenjin and Swahili, each with its own architecture and layout. In the afternoon, in a large circular auditorium, the resident troupe performs dances, songs and acrobatics from across Kenya, with drums, horns and costumes. It is a lively introduction to the diversity of a country of more than forty communities.

lad.lad-marginal: Luanda was founded in 1576 by the Portuguese Paulo Dias de Novais as São Paulo da Assunção de Loanda, around this bay protected by the sand spit of the Ilha. The Marginal, officially Avenida 4 de Fevereiro, recalls 4 February 1961, the start of the armed struggle for independence. Rebuilt in the 2010s on reclaimed land, it is now a promenade of more than three kilometres with palm trees, gardens and cycle paths, between the bay and the new towers of the city. At the end of the afternoon, Luandans come here to walk, run, skate and meet friends as the light turns gold over the water.
lad.lad-baixa: The Baixa is the old lower town of Luanda. The Church of Nossa Senhora da Nazaré was built in 1664 by the governor André Vidal de Negreiros, and inside, its blue-and-white Portuguese tiles depict the Battle of Ambuila of 1665. Nearby, on Rua Major Kanhangulo, stands the Palácio de Ferro, a prefabricated iron building of the late 19th century. It is traditionally attributed to the workshop of Gustave Eiffel, and legend says it was bound for Madagascar when the ship carrying it went off course and it ended up in Luanda. Restored, it is a reminder of the city's colonial trading past.
lad.lad-fortaleza: The Fortress of São Miguel stands on the hill where Paulo Dias de Novais founded Luanda in 1576. For centuries it was the centre of Portuguese power in Angola and a base of the slave trade to Brazil; the Dutch held it from 1641 to 1648. Its walls are lined with azulejo panels showing the history of the colony. Since 1978 it has housed the National Museum of Military History, with weapons, vehicles and aircraft from the liberation struggle and the civil war, and the bronze statues of Portuguese colonial figures moved here after independence. From the ramparts you look over the bay, the Ilha and the port.
lad.lad-memorial: The Memorial António Agostinho Neto is the mausoleum of Angola's first president, a doctor and poet who led the MPLA and proclaimed independence on 11 November 1975; he died in 1979. Construction began in the early 1980s and the memorial was inaugurated in 2012. Its 120-metre tower, visible from much of the city, stands on the Praia do Bispo shore. Inside are the tomb, a museum of his life and work, a library and exhibitions on Angolan history, and a lift to a viewing level. On 17 September, his birthday, Angola celebrates National Heroes' Day.
lad.lad-ilha: The Ilha de Luanda is not really an island but a sand spit about seven kilometres long, which shelters the bay from the Atlantic. It was the home of the Axiluanda, fishermen whose name means people of the net, and of Kianda, the water spirit of Luandan tradition who is honoured with offerings. Today the outer shore is lined with beaches, beach clubs and restaurants serving grilled fish and lobster, and on weekends the Ilha fills with music and families. At the far end you can watch the fishermen's canoes. Sunset over the Atlantic, with a cold drink, is the classic Luanda moment.
lad.lad-lua: The Miradouro da Lua, the Moon Viewpoint, lies about 40 kilometres south of Luanda on the road to Cabo Ledo. Over thousands of years, wind and rain have carved the cliffs above the ocean into ridges, gullies and pinnacles in shades of red, ochre and white, a landscape that really does look like another planet. A viewing platform sits at the edge, with the Atlantic behind. The colours are strongest in the late afternoon light. On the way you pass the Museu Nacional da Escravatura, in a 17th-century chapel where enslaved people were baptised before being shipped across the ocean.

acc.acc-nkrumah: On the night of 6 March 1957, on the old polo ground where this park now stands, Kwame Nkrumah declared that Ghana was free forever, making it the first sub-Saharan colony to win independence. The memorial park opened in 1992. Its mausoleum, clad in Italian marble, holds the tombs of Nkrumah and his wife Fathia, and the museum shows his books, photographs and the story of the Pan-African movement he led. Look for the headless bronze statue: it was knocked down after the 1966 coup that removed him, and its head was later found and placed beside it. Fountains with trumpeters frame the path.
acc.acc-jamestown: Jamestown is the oldest part of Accra, a Ga fishing community that grew around James Fort, built by the British in the 1670s, while the Dutch held Ussher Fort nearby. From the red-and-white lighthouse you look down on the harbour, where brightly painted canoes come in with the day's catch and women smoke fish along the shore. Jamestown is also the cradle of Ghanaian boxing: champions trained in its small open-air gyms. Every August the Chale Wote street art festival fills the lanes with murals, music and performances. Go with a local guide, who will open doors and explain the community.
acc.acc-makola: Makola is the commercial heart of Accra, a vast market where thousands of traders, most of them women, sell everything from wax-print fabrics and beads to yams, smoked fish, cooking pots and spices. The market women, sometimes called Makola queens, have long been a powerful economic force; the market was even demolished by the government in 1979 in a campaign against price hoarding, and later rebuilt. The lanes are packed, loud and colourful. Keep your phone and wallet close, ask before taking pictures and be ready to bargain with good humour.
acc.acc-independence: Independence Square, also called Black Star Square, was built by Kwame Nkrumah in 1961 for the visit of Queen Elizabeth II. It is one of the largest city squares in the world, used for national parades on 6 March. At one end stands the Black Star Gate, crowned with the black star of African freedom and inscribed «Freedom and Justice AD 1957»; nearby, the Independence Arch and the Eternal Flame of African Liberation, lit by Nkrumah. Behind the stands, the Atlantic rolls onto the beach. The scale of the square is a reminder of the ambitions of Africa's first independent generation.
acc.acc-osu: Osu is Accra's most lively district, and Oxford Street is its spine, lined with shops, banks, chop bars, cafés and nightclubs that stay open late. Down by the sea stands Osu Castle, also called Christiansborg, built by the Danes in 1661 as a trading fort and later used in the slave trade; after independence it was the seat of Ghana's government until 2013. In the evening the street fills with music, from highlife to Afrobeats, and with grills selling kebab-like suya and kelewele, spicy fried plantain. It is the best place to feel the energy of modern Accra.
acc.acc-labadi: Labadi Beach, also called La Pleasure Beach, is Accra's most popular beach, on the shore of the La community, one of the original Ga towns. At weekends it fills with families, drummers, dancers, acrobats and horse riders offering rides along the sand, and bars play music until the evening. In August the La people celebrate Homowo, a harvest festival whose name means hooting at hunger. The sea here has strong currents, so swim only where lifeguards are present. There is a small entrance fee, which keeps the beach cleaner than others nearby.

kgl.kgl-memorial: The Kigali Genocide Memorial stands on the hill of Gisozi, where more than 250,000 victims of the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi are buried in mass graves. In about a hundred days, from April to July 1994, hundreds of thousands of people were murdered across Rwanda. Opened in 2004, the memorial explains how the genocide was prepared and carried out, how the country began to rebuild, and includes a moving room dedicated to the children who were killed. In 2023 it became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Entry is free; allow time, move quietly, and do not photograph inside the exhibitions.
kgl.kgl-inema: Inema Arts Center was founded in 2012 by the brothers Emmanuel Nkuranga and Innocent Nkurunziza, self-taught painters who wanted to give young Rwandan artists a place to create and exhibit. The word inema means gift from God. Today its colourful walls hold a gallery of paintings, sculptures and installations, with studios where you can meet the artists at work. The style is bold and joyful, often using African patterns and recycled materials. There are also dance performances and workshops. It is a good place to understand the creative energy of the new Rwanda.
kgl.kgl-kcc: The Kigali Convention Centre, opened in 2016, has become the symbol of modern Kigali. Its spiral dome was inspired by the traditional royal palace of Nyanza, whose round thatched huts were the residence of Rwanda's kings. At night the dome lights up in changing colours, visible from the hills across the city. The centre hosts international summits, and the area around it, with the Radisson Blu hotel and wide boulevards, shows the clean, orderly city that Kigali has become. Across the road, the Kigali Heights complex has cafés with views.
kgl.kgl-kimironko: Kimironko is the largest and liveliest market in Kigali, and the best place to see daily life. Under its roofs you find mountains of fruit and vegetables, passion fruit, tree tomatoes, avocados and bananas, as well as beans, cassava flour, dried fish and baskets woven in traditional patterns. In the fabric section, traders sell kitenge cloth in bold prints, and tailors at sewing machines will make a shirt or dress to measure in a few hours. Prices are fair and haggling is gentle. Remember that plastic bags are banned in Rwanda, so bring a bag of your own.
kgl.kgl-nyamirambo: Nyamirambo is one of Kigali's oldest neighbourhoods, laid out by the Belgians in the 1920s for Swahili-speaking traders and Muslims, and it is still the most colourful and lively part of the city. Along its main street are barbers, tailors, cafés and the bright green Mosquée Verte. The Nyamirambo Women's Center, founded in 2007, runs walking tours led by local women, who take you into homes, workshops and a traditional healer's house, and teach basket weaving and cooking. In the evening the terraces fill with people eating brochettes and grilled plantain. Football is played on every patch of ground.
kgl.kgl-palace: The Presidential Palace Museum in Kanombe was the residence of President Juvénal Habyarimana. On the evening of 6 April 1994, his plane was shot down on its approach to Kigali airport and crashed into the garden of the palace; within hours the genocide against the Tutsi began. The wreckage still lies where it fell. The house, now a museum, shows the president's rooms, a secret passage and the life of the regime's elite. It is close to the airport, so it can be a final stop before your flight. There is an entrance fee for foreign visitors.

dkr.dkr-plateau: Dakar was founded by the French in 1857 and from 1902 it was the capital of French West Africa, a territory eight times the size of France. The Plateau is the old administrative centre, and the Place de l'Indépendance, formerly Place Protet, is its heart. Around the square stand the Chamber of Commerce, banks, hotels and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, while avenues lead down to the port and to the presidential palace. The square takes its name from 4 April 1960, the date of Senegal's independence, under its first president, the poet Léopold Sédar Senghor.
dkr.dkr-kermel: Marché Kermel is a round market hall first built in 1910, with an iron frame and colourful tiles in the Sudanese colonial style. It burned down in 1993 and was rebuilt in 1997 exactly as it was. Inside, traders sell fresh fish, prawns and lobster, fruit, vegetables and flowers, while the stalls around the outside sell wooden masks, baskets, fabrics and jewellery. It is calmer and more orderly than the huge Sandaga market nearby. Bargain politely, and accept that a vendor may walk with you for a while: a firm, friendly no is understood.
dkr.dkr-goree: Gorée is a small car-free island twenty minutes by ferry from Dakar, with lanes of ochre and pink houses covered in bougainvillea. From the 15th to the 19th century it was held in turn by the Portuguese, Dutch, English and French, and it became a symbol of the Atlantic slave trade. The House of Slaves, built in the 18th century, shows the cells where captives were held and the Door of No Return opening onto the ocean. Historians debate how many enslaved people actually passed through Gorée, but it is a powerful place of remembrance, visited by Nelson Mandela, popes and presidents. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.
dkr.dkr-mcn: The Museum of Black Civilisations opened in December 2018, fulfilling a dream of President Léopold Sédar Senghor, who proposed it during the First World Festival of Black Arts held in Dakar in 1966. Its round building is inspired by the traditional impluvium houses of Casamance, in southern Senegal. The collections trace the history of Africa and its diaspora, from the earliest human fossils to masks, textiles, ancient metalwork and contemporary art from across the continent and the Americas. It is one of the largest museums of its kind in Africa. Closed on Mondays.
dkr.dkr-renaissance: The African Renaissance Monument was inaugurated in 2010 for the fiftieth anniversary of Senegal's independence. Standing on one of the two Mamelles hills, it is a 49-metre bronze group of a man holding a child aloft and a woman, facing the Atlantic, taller than the Statue of Liberty. It was built by a North Korean company and has been controversial for its cost and its style, but it has become a landmark of Dakar. Climb the long staircase, almost two hundred steps, then take the lift to a viewing room in the man's head, with a panorama of the peninsula and the ocean.
dkr.dkr-almadies: The Pointe des Almadies is the westernmost point of mainland Africa, a rocky headland where the Atlantic crashes on black rocks. Around it are hotels, the restaurants of the Almadies district and simple stalls grilling fish and lobster caught that morning. Just to the east, Ngor village faces Ngor Island, five minutes away by pirogue, with small beaches and the right-hand wave that appeared in the 1966 surf film «The Endless Summer». Surf schools rent boards for every level. Watch the sun set into the ocean, the last on the continent to see it go.
